entries.855669e969214feb5bb187e043fd4132dc6214cc: <div sID="gen23137" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="21" osisID="Matt.21" sID="Matt.21"/> <div eID="gen23137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23138" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23139" type="x-p"/> The death and resurrection of Jesus Christ are the two main hinges upon which the door of salvation turns. He came into the world on purpose to give his life a ransom; so he had lately said, <reference osisRef="Matt.20.28">ch. xx. 28</reference>. And therefore the history of his sufferings, even unto death, and his rising again, is more particularly recorded by all the evangelists than any other part of his story; and to that this evangelist now hastens apace. For at this chapter begins that which is called the passion-week. He had said to his disciples more than once, Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and there the Son of man must be betrayed. A great deal of good work he did by the way, and now at length he is come up to Jerusalem; and here we have, I. The public entry which he made into Jerusalem, upon the first day of the passion-week, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.1-Matt.21.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. The authority he exercised there, in cleansing the temple, and driving out of it the buyers and sellers, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.12-Matt.21.16">ver. 12-16</reference>. III. The barren fig-tree, and his discourse with his disciples thereupon, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.17-Matt.21.22">ver. 17-22</reference>. IV. His justifying his own authority, by appealing to the baptism of John, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.23-Matt.21.27">ver. 23-27</reference>. V. His shaming the infidelity and obstinacy of the chief priests and elders, with the repentance of the publicans, illustrated by the parable of the two sons, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.29-Matt.21.32">ver. 29-32</reference>. VI. His reading the doom of the Jewish church for its unfruitfulness, in the parable of the vineyard let out to unthankful husbandmen, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.33-Matt.21.46">ver. 33-46</reference>.
entries.8bf217ca987943a71d4e467357616d758068de96: <div eID="gen23139" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23138" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Entrance into Jerusalem.</title> <div sID="gen23140" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And when they drew nigh unto Jerusalem, and were come to Bethphage, unto the mount of Olives, then sent Jesus two disciples, <hi type="super">2</hi> Saying unto them, Go into the village over against you, and straightway ye shall find an ass tied, and a colt with her: loose <hi type="italic">them,</hi> and bring <hi type="italic">them</hi> unto me. <hi type="super">3</hi> And if any <hi type="italic">man</hi> say ought unto you, ye shall say, The Lord hath need of them; and straightway he will send them. <hi type="super">4</hi> All this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, <hi type="super">5</hi> Tell ye the daughter of Sion, Behold, thy King cometh unto thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the disciples went, and did as Jesus commanded them, <hi type="super">7</hi> And brought the ass, and the colt, and put on them their clothes, and they set <hi type="italic">him</hi> thereon. 8 And a very great multitude spread their garments in the way; others cut down branches from the trees, and strawed <hi type="italic">them</hi> in the way. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the multitudes that went before, and that followed, cried, saying, Hosanna to the Son of David: Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest. <hi type="super">10</hi> And when he was come into Jerusalem, all the city was moved, saying, Who is this? <hi type="super">11</hi> And the multitude said, This is Jesus the prophet of Nazareth of Galilee. <div eID="gen23140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23141" type="x-p"/> All the four evangelists take notice of this passage of Christ's <hi type="italic">riding in triumph into Jerusalem,</hi> five days before his death. The passover was on the fourteenth day of the month, and this was the tenth; on which day the law appointed that the paschal lamb should be taken up (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.3">Exod. xii. 3</reference>), and set apart for that service; on that day therefore Christ our Passover, who was to be sacrificed for us, was publicly showed. So that this was the prelude to his passion. He had lodged at Bethany, a village not far from Jerusalem, for some time; at a supper there the night before Mary had <hi type="italic">anointed his feet,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.3">John xii. 3</reference>. But, as usual with ambassadors, he deferred his public entry till some time after his arrival. Our Lord Jesus travelled much, and his custom was to travel on foot from Galilee to Jerusalem, some scores of miles, which was both humbling and toilsome; many a dirty weary step he had when <hi type="italic">he went about doing good.</hi> How ill does it become Christians to be inordinately solicitous about their own ease and state, when their Master had so little of either! Yet once in his life he rode in triumph; and it was now when he went into Jerusalem, to suffer and die, as if that were the pleasure and preferment he courted; and then he thought himself begin to look great. <div eID="gen23141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23142" type="x-p"/> Now here we have, <div eID="gen23142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23143" type="x-p"/> I. The provision that was made for this solemnity; and it was very poor and ordinary, and such as bespoke his <hi type="italic">kingdom</hi> to be <hi type="italic">not of this world.</hi> Here were no heralds at arms provided, no trumpet sounded before him, no chariots of state, no liveries; such things as these were not agreeable to his present state of humiliation, but will be far outdone at his second coming, to which his magnificent appearance is reserved, when the last trumpet shall sound, the glorious angels shall be his heralds and attendants, and the clouds his chariots. But in this public appearance, <div eID="gen23143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23144" type="x-p"/> 1. The preparation was sudden and offhand. For his glory in the other world, and ours with him, preparation was made before the foundation of the world, for that was the glory his heart was upon; his glory in this world he was dead to, and therefore, though he had it in prospect, did not forecast for it, but took what came next. They were come to Bethphage, which was the suburb of Jerusalem, and was accounted (say the Jewish doctors) in all things, as Jerusalem, a long scattering street that lay toward the mount of Olives; when he entered upon that, <hi type="italic">he sent two of his disciples,</hi> some think Peter and John, to fetch him an ass, for he had none ready for him. <div eID="gen23144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23145" type="x-p"/> 2. It was very mean. He sent only for an ass and her colt, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.2">v. 2</reference>. Asses were much used in that country for travel; horses were kept only by great men, and for war. Christ could have summoned a cherub to carry him (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.10">Ps. xviii. 10</reference>); but though <hi type="italic">by his name Jah,</hi> which speaks him God, <hi type="italic">he rides upon the heavens,</hi> yet now by his name Jesus, <hi type="italic">Immanuel, God with us,</hi> in his state of humiliation, he <hi type="italic">rides upon an ass.</hi> Yet some think that he had herein an eye to the custom in Israel for the judges to ride upon white asses (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.10">Judg. v. 10</reference>), and their sons on ass-colts, <reference osisRef="Judg.12.14">Judg. xii. 14</reference>. And Christ would thus enter, not as a Conqueror, but as the Judge of Israel, <hi type="italic">who for judgment came into this world.</hi> <div eID="gen23145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23146" type="x-p"/> 3. It was not his own, but borrowed. Though he had not a house of his own, yet, one would think, like some wayfaring men that live upon their friends, he might have had an ass of his own, to carry him about; but for our sakes he became in all respects poor, <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.9">2 Cor. viii. 9</reference>. It is commonly said, "They that live on borrowing, live on sorrowing;" in this therefore, as in other things, Christ <hi type="italic">was a man of sorrows</hi>—that he had nothing of this world's goods but what was given him or lent him. <div eID="gen23146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23147" type="x-p"/> The disciples who were sent to borrow this ass are directed to say, <hi type="italic">The Lord has need of him.</hi> Those that are in need, must not be ashamed to own their need, nor say, as the unjust steward, <hi type="italic">To beg I am ashamed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.3">Luke xvi. 3</reference>. On the other hand, none ought to impose upon the kindness of their friends, by going to beg or borrow when they have not need. In the borrowing of this ass, <div eID="gen23147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23148" type="x-p"/> (1.) We have an instance of Christ's knowledge. Though the thing was altogether contingent, yet Christ could tell his disciples where they should find an ass tied, and a colt with her. His omniscience extends itself to the meanest of his creatures; asses and their colts, and their being bound or loosed. <hi type="italic">Doth God take care for oxen?</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.9">1 Cor. ix. 9.</reference>) No doubt he doth, and would not see Balaam's ass abused. He knows all the creatures, so as to make them serve his own purpose. <div eID="gen23148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23149" type="x-p"/> (2.) We have an instance of his power over the spirits of men. The hearts of the meanest subjects, as well as of kings, <hi type="italic">are in the hand of the Lord.</hi> Christ asserts his right to use the ass, in bidding them bring it to him; the fulness of the earth is the Lord Christ's; but he foresees some hindrance which disciples might meet with in this service; they must not take them <hi type="italic">clam et secreto—privily,</hi> but in the sight of the owner, much less <hi type="italic">vi et armis—with force and arms,</hi> but with the consent of the owner, which he undertakes they shall have; <hi type="italic">If any man say aught to you, ye shall say, The Lord hath need of him.</hi> Note, What Christ sets us to do, he will bear us out in the doing of, and furnish us with answers to the objections we may be assaulted with, and make them prevalent; as here, <hi type="italic">Straightway he will send them.</hi> Christ, in commanding the ass into his service, showed that he is Lord of hosts; and, in inclining the owner to send him without further security, showed that he is the <hi type="italic">God of the spirits of all flesh,</hi> and can bow men's hearts. <div eID="gen23149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23150" type="x-p"/> (3.) We have an example of justice and honesty, in not using the ass, though for so small a piece of service as riding the length of a street or two, without the owner's consent. As some read the latter clause, it gives us a further rule of justice; <hi type="italic">"You shall say the Lord hath need of them, and he</hi>" (that is, <hi type="italic">the Lord) "will presently send them back,</hi> and take care that they be safely delivered to the owner, as soon as he has done with them." Note, What we borrow we must restore in due time and in good order; for <hi type="italic">the wicked borrows and pays not again.</hi> Care must be taken of borrowed goods, that they be not damaged. <hi type="italic">Alas, Master, for it was borrowed!</hi> <div eID="gen23150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23151" type="x-p"/> II. The prediction that was fulfilled in this, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.4-Matt.21.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. Our Lord Jesus, in all that he did and suffered, had very much his eye upon this, <hi type="italic">That the scriptures might be fulfilled.</hi> As the prophets looked forward to him (to him they all bare witness), so he looked upon them, that all things which were written of the Messiah, might be punctually accomplished in him. This particularly which was written of him, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zech. ix. 9</reference>, where it ushers in a large prediction of the kingdom of the Messiah, <hi type="italic">Tell ye the daughter of Sion, Behold, thy King cometh,</hi> must be accomplished. Now observe here, <div eID="gen23151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23152" type="x-p"/> 1. How the coming of Christ is foretold; <hi type="italic">Tell ye the daughter of Sion,</hi> the church, the holy mountain, <hi type="italic">Behold, thy King cometh unto thee.</hi> Note, (1.) Jesus Christ is the church's King, one of our brethren like unto us, according to the law of the kingdom, <reference osisRef="Deut.17.15">Deut. xvii. 15</reference>. He is appointed King over the church, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>. He is accepted King by the church; the daughter of Sion swears allegiance to him, <reference osisRef="Hos.1.11">Hos. i. 11</reference>. (2.) Christ, the King of his church, came to his church, even in this lower world; he comes to thee, to rule thee, to rule in thee, to rule for thee; he is <hi type="italic">Head over all things to the church. He came to Sion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Rom. xi. 26</reference>), that out of Sion the law might go forth; for the church and its interests were all in all with the Redeemer. (3.) Notice was given to the church beforehand of the coming of her King; <hi type="italic">Tell the daughter of Sion.</hi> Note, Christ will have his coming looked for, and waited for, and his subjects big with expectation of it; <hi type="italic">Tell the daughters of Sion,</hi> that they may <hi type="italic">go forth, and behold King Solomon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.3.11">Cant. iii. 11</reference>. Notices of Christ's coming are usually ushered in with a <hi type="italic">Behold!</hi> A note commanding both attention and admiration; <hi type="italic">Behold thy King cometh;</hi> behold, and wonder at him, behold, and welcome him. Here is a royal progress truly admirable. Pilate, like Caiaphas, said he knew not what, in that great word (<reference osisRef="John.19.14">John xix. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Behold your King.</hi> <div eID="gen23152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23153" type="x-p"/> 2. How his coming is described. When a king comes, something great and magnificent is expected, especially when he comes to take possession of his kingdom. The King, the Lord of hosts, was seen <hi type="italic">upon a throne, high and lifted up</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Isa. vi. 1</reference>); but there is nothing of that here; <hi type="italic">Behold, he cometh to thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass.</hi> When Christ would appear in his glory, it is in his meekness, not in his majesty. <div eID="gen23153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23154" type="x-p"/> (1.) His temper is very mild. He comes not in wrath to take vengeance, but in mercy to work salvation. He is meek to suffer the greatest injuries and indignities for Sion's cause, meek to bear with the follies and unkindness of Sion's own children. He is easy of access, easy to be entreated. He is meek not only as a Teacher, but as a Ruler; he rules by love. His government is mild and gentle, and his laws not written in the blood of his subjects, but in his own. His yoke is easy. <div eID="gen23154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23155" type="x-p"/> (2.) As an evidence of this, his appearance is very mean, sitting upon an ass, as creature made not for state, but service, not for battles, but for burthens; slow in its motions, but sure, and safe, and constant. The foretelling of this so long before, and the care taken that it should be exactly fulfilled, intimate it to have a peculiar significancy, for the encouragement of poor souls to apply themselves to Christ. Sion's King comes riding, not on a prancing horse, which the timorous petitioner dares not come near, or a running horse, which the slow-footed petitioner cannot keep pace with, but on a quiet ass, that the poorest of his subjects may not be discouraged in their access to him. Mention is made in the prophecy of <hi type="italic">a colt, the foal of an ass;</hi> and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> Christ sent for the colt with the ass, that the scripture might be fulfilled. <div eID="gen23155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23156" type="x-p"/> III. The procession itself, which was answerable to the preparation, both being destitute of worldly pomp, and yet both accompanied with a spiritual power. <div eID="gen23156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23157" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. His equipage; <hi type="italic">The disciples did as Jesus commanded them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.6">v. 6</reference>); they went to fetch the ass and the colt, not doubting but to find them, and to find the owner willing to lend them. Note, Christ's commands must not be disputed, but obeyed; and those that sincerely obey them, shall not be balked or baffled in it; <hi type="italic">They brought the ass and the colt.</hi> The meanness and contemptibleness of the beast Christ rode on, might have been made up with the richness of the trappings; but those were, like all the rest, such as came next to hand; they had not so much as a saddle for the ass, but the disciples threw some of their clothes upon it, and that must serve for want of better accommodations. Note, We ought not to be nice or curious, or to affect exactness, in outward conveniences. A holy indifference or neglect well becomes us in these things: it will evidence that our heart is not upon them, and that we have learned the apostle's rule (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.16">Rom. xii. 16</reference>, margin), <hi type="italic">to be content with mean things.</hi> Any thing will serve travellers; and there is a beauty in some sort of carelessness, a noble negligence; yet the disciples furnished him with the best they had, and did not object the spoiling of their clothes when <hi type="italic">the Lord had need of them.</hi> Note, We must not think the clothes on our backs too dear to part with for the service of Christ, for the clothing of his poor destitute and afflicted members. <hi type="italic">I was naked, and you clothed me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.25.36">ch. xxv. 36</reference>. Christ stripped himself for us. <div eID="gen23157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23158" type="x-p"/> 2. His retinue; there was nothing in this stately or magnificent. Sion's King comes to Sion, and the daughter of Sion was told of his coming long before; yet he is not attended by the gentlemen of the country, nor met by the magistrates of the city in their formalities as one might have expected; he should have had the keys of the city presented to him, and should have been conducted with all possible convenience to <hi type="italic">the thrones of judgment, the thrones of the house of David;</hi> but here is nothing of all this; yet he has his attendants, <hi type="italic">a very great multitude;</hi> they were only the common people, the mob (the <hi type="italic">rabble</hi> we should have been apt to call them), that graced the solemnity of Christ's triumph, and none but such. The chief priests and the elders afterward herded themselves with the multitude that abused him upon the cross; but we find none of them here joining with the multitude that did him honour. Ye see here your calling, brethren, <hi type="italic">not many mighty, or noble,</hi> attend on Christ, but <hi type="italic">the foolish things of this world and base things, which are despised,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26">1 Cor. i. 26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">28</reference>. Note, Christ is honoured by the multitude, more than by the magnificence, of his followers; for he values men by their souls, not by their preferments, names, or titles of honour. <div eID="gen23158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23159" type="x-p"/> Now, concerning this great multitude, we are here told, <div eID="gen23159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23160" type="x-p"/> (1.) What they did; according to the best of their capacity, they studied to do honour to Christ. [1.] <hi type="italic">They spread their garments in the way,</hi> that he might ride upon them. When Jehu was proclaimed king, the captains put their garments under him, in token of their subjection to him. Note, Those that take Christ for their King must lay their all under his feet; the clothes, in token of the heart; for when Christ comes, though not when any one else comes, it must be <hi type="italic">said to the soul, Bow down, that he may go over.</hi> Some think that these garments were spread, not upon the ground, but on the hedges or walls, to adorn the roads; as, to beautify a cavalcade, the balconies are hung with tapestry. This was but a poor piece of state, yet Christ accepted their good-will; and we are hereby taught to contrive how to make Christ welcome, Christ and his grace, Christ and his gospel, into our hearts and houses. How shall we express our respects to Christ? What honour and what dignity shall be done to him? [2.] <hi type="italic">Others cut down branches from the trees, and strewed them in the way,</hi> as they used to do at the feast of tabernacles, in token of liberty, victory, and joy; for the mystery of that feast is particularly spoken of as belonging to gospel times, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zech. xiv. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen23160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23161" type="x-p"/> (2.) What they said; <hi type="italic">They that went before, and they that followed,</hi> were in the same tune; both those that gave notice of his coming, and those that attended him with their applauses, <hi type="italic">cried, saying, Hosanna to the Son of David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.9">v. 9</reference>. When they carried branches about at the feast of tabernacles, they were wont to cry <hi type="italic">Hosanna,</hi> and from thence to call their bundles of branches their <hi type="italic">hosannas. Hosanna</hi> signifies, <hi type="italic">Save now, we beseech thee;</hi> referring to <reference osisRef="Ps.118.25-Ps.118.26">Ps. cxviii. 25, 26</reference>, where the Messiah is prophesied of as the <hi type="italic">Head-stone of the corner,</hi> though <hi type="italic">the builders refused him;</hi> and all his loyal subjects are brought in triumphing with him, and attending him with hearty good wishes to the prosperity of all his enterprises. <hi type="italic">Hosanna to the Son of David</hi> is, "This we do in honour of the Son of David." <div eID="gen23161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23162" type="x-p"/> The hosannas with which Christ was attended bespeak two things: <div eID="gen23162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23163" type="x-p"/> [1.] Their welcoming his kingdom. <hi type="italic">Hosanna</hi> bespeaks the same with, <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.</hi> It was foretold concerning this Son of David, that <hi type="italic">all nations shall call him blessed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.17">Ps. lxxii. 17</reference>); these here began, and all true believers in all ages concur in it, and call him blessed; it is the genuine language of faith. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Jesus Christ <hi type="italic">comes in the name of the Lord;</hi> he is sanctified, and sent into the world, as Mediator; <hi type="italic">him hath God the Father sealed. Secondly,</hi> The coming of Christ in the name of the Lord, is <hi type="italic">worthy of all acceptation;</hi> and we all ought to say, <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that cometh;</hi> to praise him, and be pleased in him. Let his coming in the name of the Lord be mentioned with strong affections, to our comfort, and joyful acclamations, to his glory. Well may we say, <hi type="italic">Blessed is he;</hi> for it is in him that we are blessed. Well may we follow <hi type="italic">him</hi> with our blessings, who meets us with his. <div eID="gen23163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23164" type="x-p"/> [2.] Their wishing well to his kingdom; intimated in their <hi type="italic">Hosanna;</hi> earnestly desiring that prosperity and success may attend it, and that it may be a victorious kingdom; "<hi type="italic">Send now prosperity</hi> to that kingdom." If they understood it of a temporal kingdom, and had their hearts carried out thus toward that, it was their mistake, which a little time would rectify; however, their good-will was accepted. Note, It is our duty earnestly to desire and pray for the prosperity and success of Christ's kingdom in the world. Thus <hi type="italic">prayer must be made for him continually</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.15">Ps. lxxii. 15</reference>), that all happiness may attend his interest in the world, and that, though he may ride on an ass, yet in his majesty he may <hi type="italic">ride prosperously, because of</hi> that <hi type="italic">meekness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.4">Ps. xlv. 4</reference>. This we mean when we pray, <hi type="italic">Thy kingdom come.</hi> They add, <hi type="italic">Hosanna in the highest:</hi> Let prosperity in the highest degree attend him, let him have a name above every name, a throne above every throne; or, Let us praise him in the best manner for his church ascend to heaven, to the highest heavens, and fetch in peace and salvation from thence. See <reference osisRef="Ps.20.6">Ps. xx. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord saveth his Anointed, and will hear from his</hi> high, his <hi type="italic">holy heaven.</hi> <div eID="gen23164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23165" type="x-p"/> 3. We have here his entertainment in Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.10">v. 10</reference>); <hi type="italic">When he was come into Jerusalem, all the city was moved;</hi> every one took notice of him, some were moved with wonder at the novelty of the thing, others with laughter at the meanness of it; some perhaps were moved with joy, <hi type="italic">who waited for the Consolation of Israel;</hi> others, of the Pharisaical class, were moved with envy and indignation. So various are the motions in the minds of men upon the approach of Christ's kingdom! <div eID="gen23165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23166" type="x-p"/> Upon this commotion we are further told, <div eID="gen23166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23167" type="x-p"/> (1.) What the citizens said; <hi type="italic">Who is this?</hi> [1.] They were, it seems, ignorant concerning Christ. Though he was <hi type="italic">the Glory of his people Israel,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">Israel knew him not;</hi> though he had distinguished himself by the many miracles he wrought among them, yet <hi type="italic">the daughters of Jerusalem</hi> knew him not <hi type="italic">from another beloved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.5.9">Cant. v. 9</reference>. The Holy One unknown in the holy city! In places where the clearest light shines, and the greatest profession of religion is made, there is more ignorance than we are. [2.] Yet they were inquisitive concerning him. Who is this that is thus cried, and comes with so much observation? <hi type="italic">Who is this King of glory,</hi> that demands admission into our hearts? <reference osisRef="Ps.24.8">Ps. xxiv. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Isa. lxiii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen23167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23168" type="x-p"/> (2.) How the multitude answered them; <hi type="italic">This is Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.11">v. 11</reference>. The multitude were better acquainted with Christ than the great ones. <hi type="italic">Vox populi—The voice of the people,</hi> is sometimes <hi type="italic">Vox Dei—the voice of God.</hi> Now, in the account they give of him, [1.] They were right in calling him <hi type="italic">the Prophet, that great Prophet.</hi> Hitherto he had been known as a Prophet, teaching and working miracles; now they attend him as a King; Christ's priestly office was, of all the three, last discovered. [2.] Yet they missed it, in saying he was <hi type="italic">of Nazareth;</hi> and it helped to confirm some in their prejudices against him. Note, Some that are willing to honour Christ, and bear their testimony to him, yet labour under mistakes concerning him, which would be rectified if they would take pains to inform themselves.
entries.57927baf261c2d4532608ba6b59c8f1a596e415a: <div eID="gen23168" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Profaners of the Temple Punished.</title> <div sID="gen23169" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the money-changers, and the seats of them that sold doves, <hi type="super">13</hi> And said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple; and he healed them. <hi type="super">15</hi> And when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying in the temple, and saying, Hosanna to the Son of David; they were sore displeased, <hi type="super">16</hi> And said unto him, Hearest thou what these say? And Jesus saith unto them, Yea; have ye never read, Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise? 17 And he left them, and went out of the city into Bethany; and he lodged there. <div eID="gen23169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23170" type="x-p"/> When Christ came into Jerusalem, he did not go up to the court or the palace, though he came in as a King, but <hi type="italic">into the temple;</hi> for his kingdom is spiritual, and <hi type="italic">not of this world;</hi> it is in holy things that he rules, in the temple of God that he exercises authority. Now, what did he do there? <div eID="gen23170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23171" type="x-p"/> I. Thence he drove the buyers and sellers. Abuses must first be purged out, and the plants not of God's planting be plucked up, before that which is right can be established. The great Redeemer appear as a great Reformer, that turns away ungodliness, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Rom. xi. 26</reference>. Here we are told, <div eID="gen23171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23172" type="x-p"/> 1. What he did (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.12">v. 12</reference>); <hi type="italic">He cast out all them that sold and bought;</hi> he had done this once before (<reference osisRef="John.2.14-John.2.15">John ii. 14, 15</reference>), but there was occasion to do it again. Note, Buyers and sellers driven out of the temple, will return and nestle there again, if there be not a continual care and oversight to prevent it, and if the blow be not followed, and often repeated. <div eID="gen23172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23173" type="x-p"/> (1.) The abuse was, buying and selling, and changing money, in the temple. Note, Lawful things, ill timed and ill placed, may become sinful things. That which was decent enough in another place, and not only lawful, but laudable, on another day, <hi type="italic">defiles the sanctuary,</hi> and <hi type="italic">profanes the sabbath.</hi> This buying and selling, and changing money, though secular employments, yet had the pretence of being <hi type="italic">in ordine ad spiritualia—for spiritual purposes.</hi> They sold beasts for sacrifice, for the convenience of those that could more easily bring their money with them than their beast; and they changed money for those that wanted the half shekel, which was their yearly poll, or redemption-money; or, upon the bills of return; so that this might pass for the outward business of the house of God; and yet Christ will not allow of it. Note, Great corruptions and abuses come into the church by the practices of those whose <hi type="italic">gain is godliness,</hi> that is, who make worldly gain the end of their godliness, and counterfeit godliness their way to worldly gain (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.5">1 Tim. vi. 5</reference>); <hi type="italic">from such withdraw thyself.</hi> <div eID="gen23173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23174" type="x-p"/> (2.) The purging out of this abuse. Christ <hi type="italic">cast them out that sold.</hi> He did it before <hi type="italic">with a scourge of small cords</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.2.15">John ii. 15</reference>); now he did it with a look, with a frown, with a word of command. Some reckon this none of the least of Christ's miracles, that he should himself thus clear the temple, and not be opposed in it by them who by this craft got their living, and were backed in it by the priests and elders. It is an instance of his power over the spirits of men, and the hold he has of them by their own consciences. This was the only act of regal authority and coercive power that Christ did in the days of his flesh; he began with it, <reference osisRef="John.2.12-John.2.25">John ii.</reference> and here ended with it. Tradition says, that his face shone, and beams of light darted from his blessed eyes, which astonished these market-people, and compelled them to yield to his command; if so, the scripture was fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.8">Prov. xx. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">A King that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes. He overthrew the tables of the money-changers;</hi> he did not take the money to himself, but scattered it, threw it to the ground, the fittest place for it. The Jews, in Esther's time, <hi type="italic">on the spoil laid not their hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.10">Esther ix. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen23174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23175" type="x-p"/> 2. What he said, to justify himself, and to convict them (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.13">v. 13</reference>); <hi type="italic">It is written.</hi> Note, In the reformation of the church, the eye must be upon the scripture, and that must be adhered to as the rule, the pattern in the mount; and we must go no further than we can justify ourselves with, <hi type="italic">It is written.</hi> Reformation is <hi type="italic">then</hi> right, when corrupted ordinances are reduced to their primitive institution. <div eID="gen23175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23176" type="x-p"/> (1.) He shows, from a scripture prophecy, what the temple should be, and was designed to be; <hi type="italic">My house shall be called the house of prayer;</hi> which is quoted from <reference osisRef="Isa.56.7">Isa. lvi. 7</reference>. Note, All the ceremonial institutions were intended to be subservient to moral duties; the house of sacrifices was to be a house of prayer, for that was the substance and soul of all those services; the temple was in a special manner sanctified to be a house of prayer, for it was not only the place of that worship, but the medium of it, so that the prayers made in or toward that house had a particular promise of acceptance (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.21">2 Chron. vi. 21</reference>), as it was a type of Christ; therefore Daniel looked that way in prayer; and in this sense no house or place is now, or can be, a house of prayer, for Christ is our Temple; yet in some sense the appointed places of our religious assemblies may be so called, as <hi type="italic">places where prayer is wont to be made,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.16.13">Acts xvi. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen23176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23177" type="x-p"/> (2.) He shows, from a scripture reproof, how they had abused the temple, and perverted the intention of it; <hi type="italic">Ye have made it a den of thieves.</hi> This is quoted from <reference osisRef="Jer.7.11">Jer. vii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Is this house become a den of robbers in your eyes?</hi> When dissembled piety is made the cloak and cover of iniquity, it may be said that <hi type="italic">the house of prayer</hi> is become <hi type="italic">a den of thieves,</hi> in which they lurk, and shelter themselves. Markets are too often dens of thieves, so many are the corrupt and cheating practices in buying and selling; but markets in the temple are certainly so, for they rob God of his honour, the worst of thieves, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.8">Mal. iii. 8</reference>. The priests lived, and lived plentifully, upon the altar; but, not content with that, they found other ways and means to squeeze money out of the people; and therefore Christ here calls them <hi type="italic">thieves,</hi> for they exacted that which did not belong to them. <div eID="gen23177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23178" type="x-p"/> II. There, in the temple, <hi type="italic">he healed the blind and the lame,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.14">v. 14</reference>. When he had driven the buyers and sellers out of the temple, he invited the blind and lame into it; for <hi type="italic">he fills the hungry with good things, but the rich he sends empty away.</hi> Christ, in the temple, by his word there preached, and in answer to the prayers there made, heals those that are spiritually blind and lame. It is good coming to the temple, when Christ is there, who, as he shows himself jealous for the honour of his temple, in expelling those who profane it, so he shows himself gracious to those who humbly seek him. <hi type="italic">The blind and the lame</hi> were debarred David's palace (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.8">2 Sam. v. 8</reference>), but were admitted into God's house; for the state and honour of his temple lie not in those things wherein the magnificence of princes' palaces is supposed to consist; from them blind and lame must keep their distance, but from God's temple only the wicked and profane. The temple was profane and abused when it was made a market-place, but it was graced and honoured when it was made an hospital; to be doing good in God's house, is more honourable, and better becomes it, than to be getting money there. Christ's healing was a real answer to that question, <hi type="italic">Who is this</hi>? His works testified of him more than the <hi type="italic">hosannas;</hi> and his healing in the temple was the fulfilling of the promise, that <hi type="italic">the glory of the latter house should be greater than the glory of the former.</hi> <div eID="gen23178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23179" type="x-p"/> There also he silenced the offence which the chief priests and scribes took at the acclamations with which he was attended, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.15-Matt.21.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. They that should have been most forward to give him honour, were his worst enemies. <div eID="gen23179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23180" type="x-p"/> 1. They were inwardly vexed at the wonderful things that he did; they could not deny them to be true miracles, and therefore were cut to the heart with indignation at them, as <reference osisRef="Acts.4.16">Acts iv. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.33">v. 33</reference>. The works that Christ did, recommended themselves to every man's conscience. If they had any sense, they could not but own the miracle of them; and if any good nature, could not but be in love with the mercy of them: yet, because they were resolved to oppose him, for these they envied him, and bore him a grudge. <div eID="gen23180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23181" type="x-p"/> 2. They openly quarrelled at the children's hosannas; they thought that hereby an honour was given him, which did not belong to him, and that it looked like ostentation. Proud men cannot bear that honour should be done to any but to themselves, and are uneasy at nothing more than at the just praises of deserving men. Thus Saul envied David the women's songs; and "Who can stand before envy?" When Christ is most honoured, his enemies are most displeased. <div eID="gen23181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23182" type="x-p"/> Just now we had Christ preferring the blind and the lame before the buyers and sellers; now here we have him (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.16">v. 16</reference>), taking part with the children against priests and scribes. <div eID="gen23182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23183" type="x-p"/> Observe, (1.) The children were in the temple, perhaps playing there; no wonder, when the rulers make it a <hi type="italic">market-place,</hi> that the children make it a place of pastime; but we are willing to hope that many of them were worshipping there. Note, It is good to bring children betimes to the house of prayer, <hi type="italic">for of such is the kingdom of heaven.</hi> Let children be taught to keep up the form of godliness, it will help to lead them to the power of it. Christ has a tenderness for the lambs of his flock. <div eID="gen23183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23184" type="x-p"/> (2.) They were there <hi type="italic">crying Hosanna to the Son of David.</hi> This they learned from those that were grown up. Little children say and do as they hear others say, and see others do; so easily do they imitate; and therefore great care must be taken to set them good examples, and no bad ones. <hi type="italic">Maxima debetur puero reverentia—Our intercourse with the young should be conducted with the most scrupulous care.</hi> Children will learn of those that are with them, either to curse and swear, or to pray and praise. The Jews did betimes teach their children to carry branches at the feast of tabernacles, and to cry <hi type="italic">Hosanna;</hi> but God taught them here to apply it to Christ. Note, <hi type="italic">Hosanna to the Son of David</hi> well becomes the mouths of little children, who should learn young the language of Canaan. <div eID="gen23184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23185" type="x-p"/> (3.) Our Lord Jesus not only allowed it, but was very well pleased with it, and quoted a scripture which was fulfilled in it (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.2">Ps. viii. 2</reference>), or, at least, may be accommodated to it; <hi type="italic">Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise;</hi> which, some think, refers to the children's joining in the acclamations of the people, and the women's songs with which David was honoured when he returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, and therefore is very fitly applied here to the hosannas with which the Son of David was saluted, now that he was entering upon his conflict with Satan, that Goliath. Note, [1.] Christ is so far from being ashamed of the services of little children, that he takes particular notice of them (and children love to be taken notice of), and is well pleased with them. If God may be honoured by babes and sucklings, who are made to hope at the best, much more by children who are grown up to maturity and some capacity. [2.] Praise is perfected out of the mouth of such; it has a peculiar tendency to the honour and glory of God for little children to join in his praises; the praise would be accounted defective and imperfect, if they had not their share in it; which is an encouragement for children to be good betimes, and to parents to teach them to be so; the labour neither of the one nor of the other shall be in vain. In the psalm it is, <hi type="italic">Thou hast ordained strength.</hi> Note, God <hi type="italic">perfecteth praise,</hi> by <hi type="italic">ordaining strength out of the mouths of babes and sucklings.</hi> When great things are brought about by weak and unlikely instruments, God is thereby much honoured, for his <hi type="italic">strength is perfected in weakness,</hi> and the infirmities of the babes and sucklings serve for a foil to the divine power. That which follows in the psalm, <hi type="italic">That thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger,</hi> was very applicable to the priests and scribes; but Christ did not apply it to them, but left it to them to apply it. <div eID="gen23185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23186" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Christ, having thus silenced them, forsook them, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.17">v. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">He left them,</hi> in prudence, lest they should now have seized him before his hour was come; in justice, because they had forfeited the favour of his presence. By repining at Christ's praises we drive him from us. <hi type="italic">He left them</hi> as incorrigible, and he <hi type="italic">went out of the city to Bethany,</hi> which was a more quiet retired place; not so much that he might <hi type="italic">sleep</hi> undisturbed as that he might <hi type="italic">pray</hi> undisturbed. <hi type="italic">Bethany was but two little miles from Jerusalem;</hi> thither he went on foot, to show that, when he rode, it was only to <hi type="italic">fulfil the scripture.</hi> He was not lifted up with the hosannas of the people; but, as having forgot them, soon returned to his mean and toilsome way of travelling.
entries.ee795b30a3d3e11ff1ca2e2d1f128fe023f82a6c: <div eID="gen23186" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Barren Fig-Tree Cursed.</title> <div sID="gen23187" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Now in the morning as he returned into the city, he hungered. <hi type="super">19</hi> And when he saw a fig tree in the way, he came to it, and found nothing thereon, but leaves only, and said unto it, Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever. And presently the fig tree withered away. <hi type="super">20</hi> And when the disciples saw <hi type="italic">it,</hi> they marvelled, saying, How soon is the fig tree withered away! <hi type="super">21</hi> Jesus answered and said unto them, Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith, and doubt not, ye shall not only do this <hi type="italic">which is done</hi> to the fig tree, but also if ye shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; it shall be done. <hi type="super">22</hi> And all things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive. <div eID="gen23187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23188" type="x-p"/> Observe, <div eID="gen23188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23189" type="x-p"/> I. Christ <hi type="italic">returned in the morning to Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.18">v. 18</reference>. Some think that he went out of the city over-night, because none of his friends there durst entertain him, for fear of the great men; yet, having work to do there, he returned. Note, We must never be driven off from our duty either by the malice of our foes, or the unkindness of our friends. Though he knew that in this city <hi type="italic">bonds and afflictions did abide him, yet none of these things moved</hi> him. Paul followed him when he <hi type="italic">went bound in the spirit to Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.20.22">Acts xx. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen23189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23190" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">As he went, he hungered.</hi> He was a Man, and submitted to the infirmities of nature; he was an active Man, and was so intent upon his work, that he neglected his food, and came out, fasting; for <hi type="italic">the zeal of God's house</hi> did even <hi type="italic">eat him up,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">meat and drink was to do his Father's will.</hi> He was a poor Man, and had no present supply; he was a Man that pleased not himself, for he would willingly have taken up with green raw figs for his breakfast, when it was fit that he should have had something warm. <div eID="gen23190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23191" type="x-p"/> Christ <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> hungered, that he might have occasion to work this miracle, in cursing and so withering the barren fig-tree, and therein might give us an instance of his justice and his power, and both instructive. <div eID="gen23191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23192" type="x-p"/> 1. See his <hi type="italic">justice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.19">v. 19</reference>. He went to it, expecting fruit, because it had leaves; but, finding none, he sentenced it to a perpetual barrenness. The miracle had its significance, as well as others of his miracles. All Christ's miracles hitherto were wrought for the good of men, and proved the power of his grace and blessing (the sending the devils into the herd of swine was but a permission); all he did was for the benefit and comfort of his friends, none for the terror or punishment of his enemies; but now, at last, to show that <hi type="italic">all judgment is committed to him,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">he is able</hi> not only <hi type="italic">to save, but to destroy,</hi> he would give a specimen of the power of his wrath and curse; yet this not on any man, woman, or child, because <hi type="italic">the great day of his wrath is not yet come,</hi> but on an inanimate tree; that is set forth for an example; <hi type="italic">Come, learn a parable of the fig-tree,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.32">ch. xxiv. 32</reference>. The scope of it is the same with <hi type="italic">the parable of the fig-tree,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.13.6">Luke xiii. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen23192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23193" type="x-p"/> (1.) This cursing of the barren fig-tree, represents the state of hypocrites in general; and so it teaches us, [1.] That the fruit of fig-trees may justly be expected from those that have the leaves. Christ looks for the power of religion from those that make profession of it; the favour of it from those that have the show of it; grapes from the vineyard that is planted in a fruitful hill: he hungers after it, his soul <hi type="italic">desires the first ripe fruits.</hi> [2.] Christ's just expectations from flourishing professors are often frustrated and disappointed; he comes to many, seeking fruit, and finds leaves only, and he discovers it. Many have a name to live, and are not alive indeed; dote on the form of godliness, and yet deny the power of it. [3.] The sin of barrenness is justly punished with the curse and plague of barrenness; <hi type="italic">Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever.</hi> As one of the chiefest blessings, and which was the first, is, <hi type="italic">Be fruitful;</hi> so one of the saddest curses is, <hi type="italic">Be no more fruitful.</hi> Thus the sin of hypocrites is made their punishment; they <hi type="italic">would</hi> not do good, and therefore they <hi type="italic">shall</hi> do none; he that is fruitless, let him be fruitless still, and lose his honour and comfort. [4.] A false and hypocritical profession commonly withers in this world, and it is the effect of Christ's curse; the fig-tree that had no fruit, soon lost its leaves. Hypocrites may look plausible for a time, but, having no principle, <hi type="italic">no root in themselves,</hi> their profession will soon come to nothing; the gifts wither, common graces decay, the credit of the profession declines and sinks, and the falseness and folly of the pretender are manifested to all men. <div eID="gen23193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23194" type="x-p"/> (2.) It represents the state of the nation and people of the Jews in particular; they were a fig-tree planted in Christ's way, as a church. Now observe, [1.] The disappointment they gave to our Lord Jesus. He came among them, expecting to find some fruit, something that would be pleasing to him; he hungered after it; not that he <hi type="italic">desired a gift,</hi> he needed it not, <hi type="italic">but fruit that might abound to a good account.</hi> But his expectations were frustrated; he found nothing but leaves; they called <hi type="italic">Abraham their father, but did not do the works of Abraham;</hi> they professed themselves expectants of the promised Messiah, but, when he came, they did not receive and entertain him. [2.] The doom he passed upon them, <hi type="italic">that never any fruit should grow upon them</hi> or be gathered from them, as a church or as a people, <hi type="italic">from henceforward for ever.</hi> Never any good came from them (except the particular persons among them that believe), after they rejected Christ; they became worse and worse; blindness and hardness happened to them, and grew upon them, till they were unchurched, unpeopled, and undone, and their place and nation rooted up; their beauty was defaced, their privileges and ornaments, their temple, and priesthood, and sacrifices, and festivals, and all the glories of their church and state, fell like leaves in autumn. How soon did their fig-tree wither away, after they said, <hi type="italic">His blood be on us, and our children!</hi> And the Lord was righteous in it. <div eID="gen23194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23195" type="x-p"/> 2. See the <hi type="italic">power</hi> of Christ; the former is wrapped up in the figure, but this more fully discoursed of; Christ intending thereby to direct his disciples in the use of their powers. <div eID="gen23195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23196" type="x-p"/> (1.) The disciples admired the effect of Christ's curse (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.20">v. 20</reference>); <hi type="italic">They marvelled;</hi> no power could do it but his, <hi type="italic">who spake, and it was done.</hi> They marvelled at the suddenness of the thing; <hi type="italic">How soon is the fig-tree withered away!</hi> There was no visible cause of the fig-tree's withering, but it was a secret blast, a worm at the root; it was not only the leaves of it that withered, but the body of the tree; it withered away in an instant and became like a dry stick. Gospel curses are, upon this account, the most dreadful—that they work insensibly and silently, by a fire not blown, but effectually. <div eID="gen23196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23197" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ empowered them by faith to do the like (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.21-Matt.21.22">v. 21, 22</reference>); as he said (<reference osisRef="John.14.12">John xiv. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">Greater works than these shall ye do.</hi> <div eID="gen23197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23198" type="x-p"/> Observe, [1.] The description of this wonder-working faith; <hi type="italic">If ye have faith, and doubt not.</hi> Note, Doubting of the power and promise of God is the great thing that spoils the efficacy and success of faith. "If you have faith, and dispute not" (so some read it), "dispute not with yourselves, dispute not with the promise of God; if you <hi type="italic">stagger not at the promise</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.20">Rom. iv. 20</reference>); for, as far as we do so, our faith is deficient; as certain as the promise is, so confident our faith should be. <div eID="gen23198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23199" type="x-p"/> [2.] The power and prevalence of it expressed figuratively; <hi type="italic">If ye shall say to this mountain,</hi> meaning the mount of Olives, <hi type="italic">Be thou removed, it shall be done.</hi> There might be a particular reason for his saying so of this mountain, for there was a prophecy, that <hi type="italic">the mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem, should cleave in the midst, and then remove,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.14.4">Zech. xiv. 4</reference>. Whatever was the intent of that word, the same must be the expectation of faith, how impossible soever it might appear to sense. But this is a proverbial expression; intimating that we are to believe that nothing is impossible with God, and therefore that what he has promised shall certainly be performed, though to us it seem impossible. It was among the Jews a usual commendation of their learned Rabbin, that they were removers of mountains, that is, could solve the greatest difficulties; now this may be done by faith acted on the word of God, which will bring great and strange things to pass. <div eID="gen23199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23200" type="x-p"/> [3.] The way and means of exercising this faith, and of doing that which is to be done by it; <hi type="italic">All things whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive.</hi> Faith is the soul, prayer is the body; both together make a complete man for any service. Faith, if it be right, will excite prayer; and prayer is not right, if it do not spring from faith. This is the condition of our receiving—we must <hi type="italic">ask in prayer, believing.</hi> The requests of prayer shall not be denied; the expectations of faith shall not be frustrated. We have many promises to this purport from the mouth of our Lord Jesus, and all to encourage faith, the principal grace, and prayer, the principal duty, of a Christian. It is but ask and have, believe and receive; and what would we more? Observe, How comprehensive the promise is—<hi type="italic">all things whatsoever ye shall ask;</hi> this is like all and every the premises in a conveyance. <hi type="italic">All things,</hi> in general; <hi type="italic">whatsoever,</hi> brings it to particulars; though generals include particulars, yet such is the folly of our unbelief, that, though we think we assent to promises in the general, yet we fly off when it comes to particulars, and therefore, <hi type="italic">that we might have strong consolation,</hi> it is thus copiously expressed, <hi type="italic">All things whatsoever.</hi>
entries.20d8f0703e5f19335383008289022481e7613ccd: <div eID="gen23200" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Questioned as to His Authority.</title> <div sID="gen23201" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> And when he was come into the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came unto him as he was teaching, and said, By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority? <hi type="super">24</hi> And Jesus answered and said unto them, I also will ask you one thing, which if ye tell me, I in like wise will tell you by what authority I do these things. <hi type="super">25</hi> The baptism of John, whence was it? from heaven, or of men? And they reasoned with themselves, saying, If we shall say, From heaven; he will say unto us, Why did ye not then believe him? 26 But if we shall say, Of men; we fear the people; for all hold John as a prophet. <hi type="super">27</hi> And they answered Jesus, and said, We cannot tell. And he said unto them, Neither tell I you by what authority I do these things. <div eID="gen23201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23202" type="x-p"/> Our Lord Jesus (like St. Paul after him) preached his gospel <hi type="italic">with much contention;</hi> his first appearance was in a dispute with <hi type="italic">the doctors in the temple, when he was twelve years old;</hi> and here, just before he died, we have him engaged in controversy. In this sense, he was like Jeremiah, <hi type="italic">a man of contention; not striving, but striven with.</hi> The great contenders with him, were, <hi type="italic">the chief priests and the elders,</hi> the judges of two distinct courts: the chief priests presided in the ecclesiastical court, in all matters of the Lord, as they are called; the elders of the people were judges of the civil courts, in temporal matters. See an idea of both, <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.5">2 Chron. xix. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.8">8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.11">11</reference>. These joined to attack Christ thinking they should find or make him obnoxious either to the one or to the other. See how woefully degenerate that generation was, when the governors both in church and state, who should have been the great promoters of the Messiah's kingdom, were the great opposers of it! Here we have them disturbing him when he was preaching, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.23">v. 23</reference>. They would neither receive his instructions themselves, nor let others receive them. Observe, <div eID="gen23202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23203" type="x-p"/> I. As soon as he came into Jerusalem, he went to the temple, though he had been affronted there the day before, was there in the midst of enemies and in the mouth of danger; yet thither he went, for there he had a fairer opportunity of doing good to souls than any where else in Jerusalem. Though he came hungry to the city, and was disappointed of a breakfast at the barren fig-tree, yet, for aught that appears, he went straight to the temple, as one that <hi type="italic">esteemed the words of God's mouth,</hi> the preaching of them, <hi type="italic">more than his necessary food.</hi> <div eID="gen23203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23204" type="x-p"/> II. In the temple he was teaching; he had called it <hi type="italic">a house of prayer</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.13">v. 13</reference>), and here we have him preaching there. Note, In the solemn assemblies of Christians, praying and preaching must go together, and neither must encroach upon, or jostle out, the other. To make up communion with God, we must not only speak to him in prayer, but hear what he has to say to us by his word; ministers must <hi type="italic">give themselves both to the word and to prayer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.6.4">Acts vi. 4</reference>. Now that Christ <hi type="italic">taught in the temple,</hi> that scripture was fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let us go up to the house of the Lord, and he will teach us his ways.</hi> The priests of old often taught there <hi type="italic">the good knowledge of the Lord;</hi> but they never had such a teacher as this. <div eID="gen23204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23205" type="x-p"/> III. When Christ was teaching the people, the priests and elders came upon him, and challenged him to produce his orders; the hand of Satan was in this, to hinder him in his work. Note, It cannot but be a trouble to a faithful minister, to be taken off, or diverted from, plain and practical preaching, by an unavoidable necessity of engaging in controversies, yet good was brought out of this evil, for hereby occasion was given to Christ to dispel the objections that were advanced against him, to the greater satisfaction of his followers; and, while his adversaries thought by their power to have silenced him, he by his wisdom silenced them. <div eID="gen23205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23206" type="x-p"/> Now, in this dispute with them, we may observe, <div eID="gen23206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23207" type="x-p"/> 1. How he was assaulted by their insolent demand; <hi type="italic">By what authority doest thou these things, and who gave thee this authority?</hi> Had they duly considered his miracles, and the power by which he wrought them, they needed not to have asked this question; but they must have something to say for the shelter of an obstinate infidelity. "Thou ridest in triumph into Jerusalem, receivest the hosannas of the people, controllest in the temple, drivest out such as had license to be there, from the rulers of the temple, and paid them rent; thou are here preaching a new doctrine; whence hadst thou a commission to do all this? Was it from Cæsar, or from the high priest, or from God? Produce thy warrant, thy credentials. Dost not thou take too much upon thee?" Note, It is good for all that take upon them to act with authority, to put this question to themselves, "Who gave us that authority?" For, unless a man be clear in his own conscience concerning that, he cannot act with any comfort or hope of success. They who run before their warrant, run without their blessing, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.21-Jer.23.22">Jer. xxiii. 21, 22</reference>. <div eID="gen23207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23208" type="x-p"/> Christ had often said it, and proved it beyond contradiction, and Nicodemus, a master in Israel, had owned it, that he was <hi type="italic">a teacher sent of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.2">John iii. 2</reference>); yet, at this time of day, when that point had been so fully cleared and settled, they come to him with this question. (1.) In the ostentation of their own power, as chief priests and elders, which they thought authorized them to call him to an account in this manner. How haughtily do they ask, <hi type="italic">Who gave thee this authority?</hi> Intimating that he could have no authority, because he had none from them, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.24">1 Kings xxii. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.20.1">Jer. xx. 1</reference>. Note, It is common for the greatest abusers of their power to be the most rigorous assertors of it, and to take a pride and pleasure in any thing that looks like the exercise of it. (2.) It was to ensnare and entangle him. Should he refuse to answer this question, they would enter judgment against him upon <hi type="italic">Nihil dicit—He says nothing;</hi> would condemn him as standing mute; and would insinuate to the people, that his silence was a tacit confessing of himself to be a usurper: should he plead an authority from God, they would, as formerly, demand a sign from heaven, or make his <hi type="italic">de</hi>fence his <hi type="italic">of</hi>fence, and accuse him of blasphemy for it. <div eID="gen23208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23209" type="x-p"/> 2. How he answered this demand with another, which would help them to answer it themselves (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.24-Matt.21.25">v. 24, 25</reference>); <hi type="italic">I also will ask you one thing.</hi> He declined giving them a direct answer, lest they should take advantage against him; but answers them with a question. Those that are <hi type="italic">as sheep in the midst of wolves,</hi> have need to <hi type="italic">be wise as serpents: the heart of the wise studieth to answer.</hi> We must <hi type="italic">give a reason of the hope that is in us,</hi> not only <hi type="italic">with meekness, but with fear</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1 Pet. iii. 15</reference>), with prudent caution, lest truth be damaged, or ourselves endangered. <div eID="gen23209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23210" type="x-p"/> Now this question is concerning John's baptism, here put for his whole ministry, preaching as well as baptizing; "Was this <hi type="italic">from heaven, or of men?</hi> One of the two it must be; either what he did was of his own head, or he was sent of God to do it." Gamaliel's argument turned upon this hinge (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.38-Acts.5.39">Acts v. 38, 39</reference>); either <hi type="italic">this counsel is of men or of God.</hi> Though that which is manifestly bad cannot be of God, yet that which is seemingly good may be of men, nay of Satan, when <hi type="italic">he transforms himself into an angel of light.</hi> This question was not at all shuffling, to evade theirs; but, <div eID="gen23210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23211" type="x-p"/> (1.) If they answered this question, it would answer theirs: should they say, against their consciences, that John's baptism was of men, yet it would be easy to answer, <hi type="italic">John did no miracle</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.10.41">John x. 41</reference>), Christ did many; but should they say, as they could not but own, that John's baptism was from heaven (which was supposed in the questions sent him, <reference osisRef="John.1.21">John i. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">Art thou Elias, or that prophet?</hi>) then their demand was answered, for he bare testimony to Christ. Note, Truths appear in the clearest light when they are taken in their due order; the resolving of the <hi type="italic">previous</hi> questions will be a key to the <hi type="italic">main</hi> question. <div eID="gen23211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23212" type="x-p"/> (2.) If they refused to answer it, that would be a good reason why he should not offer proofs of his authority to men that were obstinately prejudiced against the strongest conviction; it was but to cast pearls before swine. Thus <hi type="italic">he taketh the wise in their own craftiness</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.19">1 Cor. iii. 19</reference>); and those that would not be convinced of the plainest truths, shall be convicted of the vilest malice, against John first, then against Christ, and in both against God. <div eID="gen23212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23213" type="x-p"/> 3. How they were hereby baffled and run aground; they knew the truth, but would not own it, and so were taken in the snare they laid for our Lord Jesus. Observe, <div eID="gen23213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23214" type="x-p"/> (1.) How <hi type="italic">they reasoned with themselves,</hi> not concerning the merits of the cause, what proofs there were of the divine original of John's baptism; no, their care was, how to make their part good against Christ. Two things they considered and consulted, in this reasoning with themselves—their credit, and their safety; the same things which <hi type="italic">they</hi> principally aim at, who <hi type="italic">seek their own things.</hi> <div eID="gen23214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23215" type="x-p"/> [1.] They consider their own credit, which they would endanger if they should own John's baptism to be of God; for then Christ would ask them, before all the people. <hi type="italic">Why did ye not believe him?</hi> And to acknowledge that a doctrine is from God, and yet not to receive and entertain it, is the greatest absurdity and iniquity that a man can be charged with. Many that will not be kept by the fear of sin from neglecting and opposing that which they know to be true and good are kept by the fear of shame from owning that to be true and good which they neglect and oppose. Thus they <hi type="italic">reject the counsel of God against themselves,</hi> in not submitting to John's baptism, and are left without excuse. <div eID="gen23215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23216" type="x-p"/> [2.] They consider their own safety, that they would expose themselves to the resentments of the people, if they should say that John's baptism was of men; <hi type="italic">We fear the people, for all hold John as a prophet.</hi> It seems, then, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the people had truer sentiments of John than the chief priests and the elders had, or, at least, were more free and faithful in declaring their sentiments. This people, of whom they said in their pride that they <hi type="italic">knew not the law, and were cursed</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.49">John vii. 49</reference>), it seems, knew the gospel, and were blessed. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That the chief priests and elders stood in awe of the common people, which is an evidence that things were in disorder among them, and that mutual jealousies were at a great height; that the government was become obnoxious to the hatred and scorn of the people, and the scripture was fulfilled, <hi type="italic">I have made you contemptible and base,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.8-Mal.2.9">Mal. ii. 8, 9</reference>. If they had kept their integrity, and done their duty, they had kept up their authority, and needed not to fear the people. We find sometimes that the people feared them, and it served them for a reason why they did not confess Christ, <reference osisRef="John.9.22">John ix. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.12.42">xii. 42</reference>. Note, Those could not but fear the people, who studied only how to make the people fear them. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That it is usually the temper even of common people to be zealous for the honour of that which they account sacred and divine. If they <hi type="italic">account John as a prophet,</hi> they will not endure that it should be said, <hi type="italic">His baptism was of men;</hi> hence the hottest contests have been about holy things. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> That the chief priests and elders were kept from an open denial of the truth, even against the conviction of their own minds, not by the fear of God, but purely by the fear of the people; as the <hi type="italic">fear of man</hi> may <hi type="italic">bring</hi> good people into <hi type="italic">a snare</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.29.25">Prov. xxix. 25</reference>), so sometimes it may keep bad people from being <hi type="italic">overmuch wicked, lest they should die before their time,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.17">Eccl. vii. 17</reference>. Many bad people would be much worse than they are, if they durst. <div eID="gen23216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23217" type="x-p"/> (2.) How they replied to our Saviour, and so dropped the question. They fairly confessed <hi type="italic">We cannot tell;</hi> that is, "We will not;" <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ouk oi damen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">We never knew.</hi> The more shame for them, while they pretended to be leaders of the people, and by their office were obliged to take cognizance of such things; when they would not confess their knowledge, they were constrained to confess their ignorance. And observe, by the way, when they said, <hi type="italic">We cannot tell,</hi> they told a lie, for they knew that John's baptism was of God. Note, There are many who are more afraid of the <hi type="italic">shame</hi> of lying than of the <hi type="italic">sin,</hi> and therefore scruple not to speak that which they know to be false concerning their own thoughts and apprehensions, their affections and intentions, or their remembering or forgetting of things, because in those things they know nobody can disprove them. <div eID="gen23217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23218" type="x-p"/> Thus Christ avoided the snare they laid for him, and justified himself in refusing to gratify them; <hi type="italic">Neither tell I you by what authority I do these things.</hi> If they be so wicked and base as either not to believe, or not to confess, that the baptism of John was from heaven (though it obliged to repentance, that great duty, and sealed the kingdom of God at hand, that great promise), they were not fit to be discoursed with concerning Christ's authority; for men of such a disposition could not be convinced of the truth, nay, they could not but be provoked by it, and therefore <hi type="italic">he that is thus ignorant, let him be ignorant still.</hi> Note, Those that imprison the truths they know, in unrighteousness (either by not professing them, or by not practising according to them), are justly denied the further truths they enquire after, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.18-Rom.1.19">Rom. i. 18, 19</reference>. Take away the talent from him that buried it; those that <hi type="italic">will not</hi> see, <hi type="italic">shall not</hi> see.
entries.5e02f515380bd38140685fbcbb55fd31d90aebb6: <div eID="gen23218" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Parable of the Two Sons.</title> <div sID="gen23219" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> But what think ye? A <hi type="italic">certain</hi> man had two sons; and he came to the first, and said, Son, go work to day in my vineyard. <hi type="super">29</hi> He answered and said, I will not: but afterward he repented, and went. <hi type="super">30</hi> And he came to the second, and said likewise. And he answered and said, I <hi type="italic">go,</hi> sir: and went not. <hi type="super">31</hi> Whether of them twain did the will of <hi type="italic">his</hi> father? They say unto him, The first. Jesus saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you. <hi type="super">32</hi> For John came unto you in the way of righteousness, and ye believed him not: but the publicans and the harlots believed him: and ye, when ye had seen <hi type="italic">it,</hi> repented not afterward, that ye might believe him. <div eID="gen23219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23220" type="x-p"/> As Christ instructed his disciples by parables, which made the instructions the more easy, so sometimes he convinced his adversaries by parables, which bring reproofs more close, and make men, or ever they are aware, to reprove themselves. Thus Nathan convinced David by a parable (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1">2 Sam. xxii. 1</reference>), and the woman of Tekoa surprised him in like manner, <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.2">2 Sam. xiv. 2</reference>: Reproving parables are appeals to the offenders themselves, and judge them out of their own mouths. This Christ designs here, as appears by the first words (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.28">v. 28</reference>), <hi type="italic">But what think you?</hi> <div eID="gen23220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23221" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have the parable of the <hi type="italic">two sons</hi> sent to work in the vineyard, the scope of which is to show that they who knew not John's baptism to be of God, were shamed even by the publicans and harlots, who knew it, and owned it. Here is, <div eID="gen23221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23222" type="x-p"/> I. The parable itself, which represents two sorts of persons; some that prove better than they promise, represented by the first of those sons; others that promise better than they prove represented by the second. <div eID="gen23222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23223" type="x-p"/> 1. They had both one and the same father, which signifies that God is a common Father to all mankind. There are favours which all alike receive from him, and obligations which all alike lie under to him; <hi type="italic">Have we not all one Father?</hi> Yes, and yet there is a vast difference between men's characters. <div eID="gen23223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23224" type="x-p"/> 2. They had both the same command given them; <hi type="italic">Son, go work to-day in my vineyard.</hi> Parents should not breed up their children in idleness; nothing is more pleasing, and yet nothing more pernicious, to youth than that. <reference osisRef="Lam.3.27">Lam. iii. 27</reference>. God sets his children to work, though they are all heirs. This command is given to every one of us. Note, (1.) The work of religion, which we are called to engage in, is vineyard work, creditable, profitable, and pleasant. By the sin of Adam we were turned out to work upon the common, and to eat the herb of the field; but by the grace of our Lord Jesus we are called to work again in the vineyard. (2.) The gospel call to work in the vineyard, requires present obedience; <hi type="italic">Son, go work</hi> to-day, while it is called to-day, because <hi type="italic">the night comes when no man can work.</hi> We were not sent into the world to be idle, nor had we daylight given us to play by; and therefore, if ever we mean to do any thing for God and our souls, why not now? Why not to-day? (3.) The exhortation to go <hi type="italic">work to-day in the vineyard,</hi> speaketh unto us <hi type="italic">as unto children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.5">Heb. xii. 5</reference>); <hi type="italic">Son, go work.</hi> It is the command of a Father, which carries with it both authority and affection, a Father that pities his children, and considers their frame, and will not overtask them (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.13-Ps.103.14">Ps. ciii. 13, 14</reference>), a Father that is very tender of <hi type="italic">his Son that serves him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.17">Mal. iii. 17</reference>. If we work in our Father's vineyard, we work for ourselves. <div eID="gen23224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23225" type="x-p"/> 3. Their conduct was very different. <div eID="gen23225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23226" type="x-p"/> (1.) One of the sons did better than he said, proved better than he promised.
