His answer was bad, but his actions were good. <div eID="gen23226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23227" type="x-p"/> [1.] Here is the untoward answer that he gave to his father; he said, flat and plain <hi type="italic">I will not.</hi> See to what a degree of impudence the corrupt nature of man rises, to say, <hi type="italic">I will not,</hi> to the command of a Father; such a command of such a Father; they are impudent children, and stiff-hearted. Those that will not bend, surely they cannot blush; if they had any degree of modesty left them, they could not say, <hi type="italic">We will not.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.2.25">Jer. ii. 25</reference>. Excuses are bad, but downright denials are worse; yet such peremptory refusals do the calls of the gospel often meet with. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Some love their ease, and will not work; they would live in the world as leviathan in the waters, to play therein (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.26">Ps. civ. 26</reference>); they do not love working. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Their hearts are so much upon their own fields, that they are not for working in God's vineyard. They love the business of the world better than the business of their religion. Thus some by the delights of sense, and others by the employments of the world, are kept from doing that great work which they were sent into the world about, and so <hi type="italic">stand all the day idle.</hi> <div eID="gen23227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23228" type="x-p"/> [2.] Here is the happy change of his mind, and of his way, upon second thought; <hi type="italic">Afterward he repented, and went.</hi> Note, There are many who in the beginning are wicked and wilful, and very unpromising, who afterward repent and mend, and come to something. Some that God hath chosen, are suffered for a great while to run to a great excess of riot; <hi type="italic">Such were some of you,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1 Cor. vi. 11</reference>. These are set forth for <hi type="italic">patterns of long-suffering,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.16">1 Tim. i. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Afterward he repented.</hi> Repentance is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">metanoia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">an after-wit:</hi> and <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">metameleia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">an after-care.</hi> Better late than never. Observe, When he repented he went; that was the <hi type="italic">fruit meet for repentance.</hi> The only evidence of our repentance for our former resistance, is, immediately to comply, and set to work; and then what is past, shall be pardoned, and all shall be well. See what a kind Father God is; he resents not the affront of our refusals, as justly he might. He that told his father to his face, that he <hi type="italic">would not</hi> do as he bid him, deserved to be turned out of doors, and disinherited; but our God <hi type="italic">waits to be gracious,</hi> and, not withstanding our former follies, if we repent and mend, will favourably accept of us; blessed be God, we are under a covenant that leaves room for such a repentance. <div eID="gen23228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23229" type="x-p"/> (2.) The other son said better than he did, promised better than he proved; his answer was good but his actions bad. To him the father <hi type="italic">said likewise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.30">v. 30</reference>. The gospel call, though very different, is, in effect, the same to all, and is carried on with an even tenour. We have all the same commands, engagements, encouragements, though to some they are a savour of life unto life, to others of death unto death. Observe, <div eID="gen23229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23230" type="x-p"/> [1.] How fairly this other son promised; <hi type="italic">He said, I go, sir.</hi> He gives his father a title of respect, <hi type="italic">sir.</hi> Note, It becomes children to speak respectfully to their parents. It is one branch of that honour which the fifth commandment requires. He professes a ready obedience, <hi type="italic">I go;</hi> not, "I will go by and by," but, "Ready, sir, you may depend upon it, I go just now." This answer we should give from the heart heartily to all the calls and commands of the word of God. See <reference osisRef="Jer.3.22">Jer. iii. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.8">Ps. xxvii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen23230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23231" type="x-p"/> [2.] How he failed in the performance; <hi type="italic">He went not.</hi> Note, There are many that give good words, and make fair promises, in religion, and those from some good motions for the present, that rest there, and go no further, and so come to nothing. Saying and doing are two things; and many there are that say, and do not; it is particularly charged upon the Pharisees, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.3">ch. xxiii. 3</reference>. Many with their mouth show much love, but their heart goes another way. They had a good mind to be religious, but they met with something to be done, that was too hard, or something to be parted with, that was too dear, and so their purposes are to no purpose. Buds and blossoms are not fruit. <div eID="gen23231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23232" type="x-p"/> II. A general appeal upon the parable; <hi type="italic">Whether of them twain did the will of his father?</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.31">v. 31</reference>. They both had their faults, one was rude and the other was false, such variety of exercises parents sometimes have in the different humours of their children, and they have need of a great deal of wisdom and grace to know what is the best way of managing them. But the question is, Which was the better of the two, and the less faulty? And it was soon resolved; the first, because his actions were better than his words, and his latter end than his beginning. This they had learned from the common sense of mankind, who would much rather deal with one that will be better than his word, than with one that will be false to his word. And, in the intention of it, they had learned from the account God gives of the rule of his judgment (<reference osisRef="Ezek.18.21-Ezek.18.24">Ezek. xviii. 21-24</reference>), that if <hi type="italic">the sinner turn from his wickedness,</hi> he shall be pardoned; and <hi type="italic">if the righteous man turn from his righteousness,</hi> he shall be rejected. The tenour of the whole scripture gives us to understand that those are accepted as doing their Father's will, who, wherein they have missed it, are sorry for it, and do better. <div eID="gen23232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23233" type="x-p"/> III. A particular application of it to the matter in hand, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.31-Matt.21.32">v. 31, 32</reference>. The primary scope of the parable is, to show how the publicans and harlots, who never talked of the Messiah and his kingdom, yet entertained the doctrine, and submitted to the discipline, of John the Baptist, his forerunner, when the priests and elders, who were big with expectations of the Messiah, and seemed very ready to go into his measures, slighted John the Baptist, and ran counter to the designs of his mission. But it has a further reach; the Gentiles were <hi type="italic">sometimes disobedient,</hi> had been long so, children of disobedience, like the elder son (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.3-Titus.3.4">Tit. iii. 3, 4</reference>); yet, when the gospel was preached to them, they became obedient to the faith; whereas the Jews who said, <hi type="italic">I go, sir,</hi> promised fair (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.7">Exod. xxiv. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.24.24">Josh. xxiv. 24</reference>); yet went not; they did but flatter God with their mouth. <reference osisRef="Ps.78.36">Ps. lxxviii. 36</reference>. <div eID="gen23233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23234" type="x-p"/> In Christ's application of this parable, observe. <div eID="gen23234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23235" type="x-p"/> 1. How he proves that John's baptism was <hi type="italic">from heaven, and not of men.</hi> "If you <hi type="italic">cannot</hi> tell," saith Christ, "you <hi type="italic">might</hi> tell," <div eID="gen23235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23236" type="x-p"/> (1.) By the scope of his ministry; <hi type="italic">John came unto you in the way of righteousness.</hi> Would you know whether John had his commission from heaven, remember the rule of trial, <hi type="italic">By their fruits ye shall know them;</hi> the fruits of their doctrines, the fruits of their doings. Observe but their way, and you may trace out both their rise and their tendency. Now it was evident that John came <hi type="italic">in the way of righteousness.</hi> In his ministry, he taught people to repent, and to work the works of righteousness. In his conversation, he was a great example of strictness, and seriousness, and contempt of the world, denying himself, and doing good to every body else. Christ <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> submitted to the baptism of John, because it <hi type="italic">became him to fulfil all righteousness.</hi> Now, if John thus came in the way of righteousness, could they be ignorant that his baptism was from heaven, or make any doubt of it? <div eID="gen23236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23237" type="x-p"/> (2.) By the success of his ministry; <hi type="italic">The publicans and the harlots believed him;</hi> he did abundance of good among the worst sort of people. St. Paul proves his apostleship by the seals of his ministry, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.2">1 Cor. ix. 2</reference>. If God had not sent John the Baptist, he would not have crowned his labours with such wonderful success, nor have made him so instrumental as he was for the conversion of souls. If publicans and harlots believe his report, surely the arm of the Lord is with him. The people's profiting is the minister's best testimonial. <div eID="gen23237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23238" type="x-p"/> 2. How he reproves them for their contempt of John's baptism, which yet, for fear of the people, they were not willing to own. To shame them for it, he sets before them the faith, repentance, and obedience, of the publicans and harlots, which aggravated their unbelief and impenitence. As he shows, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.21">ch. xi. 21</reference>, that the less likely would have repented, so here that the less likely did repent. <div eID="gen23238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23239" type="x-p"/> (1.) The publicans and harlots were like the first son in the parable, from whom little of religion was expected. They promised little good, and those that knew them promised themselves little good from them. Their disposition was generally rude, and their conversation profligate and debauched; and yet many of them were wrought upon the by the ministry of John, who came in the spirit and power of Elias. See <reference osisRef="Luke.7.29">Luke vii. 29</reference>. These fitly represented the Gentile world; for, as Dr. Whitby observes, the Jews generally ranked the publicans with the heathen; nay, and the heathen were represented by the Jews as harlots, and born of harlots, <reference osisRef="John.8.41">John viii. 41</reference>. <div eID="gen23239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23240" type="x-p"/> (2.) The scribes and Pharisees, the chief priests and elders, and indeed the Jewish nation in general, were like the other son that gave good words; they made a specious profession of religion, and yet, when the kingdom of the Messiah was brought among them by the baptism of John, they slighted it, they turned their back upon it, nay they <hi type="italic">lifted up the heel against it.</hi> A hypocrite is more hardly convinced and converted than a gross sinner; the form of godliness, if that be rested in, becomes one of Satan's strongholds, by which he opposes the power of godliness. It was an aggravation of their unbelief, [1.] That John was such an excellent person, that he came, and came to them, in <hi type="italic">the way of righteousness.</hi> The better the means are, the greater will the account be, if not improved. [2.] That, when they saw the publicans and harlots go before them into the kingdom of heaven, they did not afterward repent and believe; were not thereby provoked to a holy emulation, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.14">Rom. xi. 14</reference>. Shall publicans and harlots go away with grace and glory; and shall not we put in for a share? Shall our inferiors be more holy and more happy than we? They had not the wit and grace that Esau had, who was moved to take other measures than he had done, by the example of his younger brother, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.6">Gen. xxviii. 6</reference>. These proud priests, that set up for leaders, scorned to follow, though it were into the kingdom of heaven, especially to follow publicans; through the pride of their countenance, they would not seek after God, after Christ, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Ps. x. 4</reference>.
entries.54cbf567287bec2849c7dbf78ec559f84e247532: <div eID="gen23240" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Parable of the Wicked Husbandmen.</title> <div sID="gen23241" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> Hear another parable: There was a certain householder, which planted a vineyard, and hedged it round about, and digged a winepress in it, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country: <hi type="super">34</hi> And when the time of the fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the husbandmen, that they might receive the fruits of it. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the husbandmen took his servants, and beat one, and killed another, and stoned another. <hi type="super">36</hi> Again, he sent other servants more than the first: and they did unto them likewise. <hi type="super">37</hi> But last of all he sent unto them his son, saying, They will reverence my son. <hi type="super">38</hi> But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance. <hi type="super">39</hi> And they caught him, and cast <hi type="italic">him</hi> out of the vineyard, and slew <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <hi type="super">40</hi> When the lord therefore of the vineyard cometh, what will he do unto those husbandmen? <hi type="super">41</hi> They say unto him, He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out <hi type="italic">his</hi> vineyard unto other husbandmen, which shall render him the fruits in their seasons. <hi type="super">42</hi> Jesus saith unto them, Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes? <hi type="super">43</hi> Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof. <hi type="super">44</hi> And whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder. <hi type="super">45</hi> And when the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables, they perceived that he spake of them. <hi type="super">46</hi> But when they sought to lay hands on him, they feared the multitude, because they took him for a prophet. <div eID="gen23241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23242" type="x-p"/> This parable plainly sets forth the sin and ruin of the Jewish nation; they and their leaders are the husbandmen here; and what is spoken for conviction to them, is spoken for caution to all that enjoy the privileges of the visible church, not to be high-minded, but fear. <div eID="gen23242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23243" type="x-p"/> I. We have here the privileges of the Jewish church, represented by the letting out of a vineyard to the husbandmen; they were as tenants holding by, from, and under, God the great Householder. Observe, <div eID="gen23243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23244" type="x-p"/> 1. How God established a church for himself in the world. The kingdom of God upon earth is here compared to a vineyard, furnished with all things requisite to an advantageous management and improvement of it. (1.) He planted this vineyard. The church is <hi type="italic">the planting of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa. lxi. 3</reference>. The forming of a church is a work by itself, like the planting of a vineyard, which requires a great deal of cost and care. It is <hi type="italic">the vineyard which his right hand has planted</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.15">Ps. lxxx. 15</reference>), planted with the <hi type="italic">choicest vine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Isa. v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">a noble vine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.2.21">Jer. ii. 21</reference>. The earth of itself produces thorns and briars; but vines must be planted. The being of a church is owing to God's distinguishing favour, and his manifesting himself to some, and not to others. (2.) He hedged it round about. Note, God's church in the world is taken under his special protection. It is <hi type="italic">a hedge round about,</hi> like that about Job on every side (<reference osisRef="Job.1.10">Job i. 10</reference>), a wall of fire, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">Zech. ii. 5</reference>. Wherever God has a church, it is, and will always be, his peculiar care. The covenant of circumcision and the ceremonial law were a hedge or a wall of partition about the Jewish church, which is taken down by Christ; who yet has appointed a gospel order and discipline to be the hedge of his church. He will not have his vineyard to lie in common, that those who are without, may thrust in at pleasure; not to lie at large, that those who are within, may lash out at pleasure; but care is taken to set bounds about this holy mountain. (3.) He <hi type="italic">digged a wine-press and built a tower.</hi> The altar of burnt-offerings was the wine-press, to which all the offerings were brought. God instituted ordinances in his church, for the due oversight of it, and for the promoting of its fruitfulness. What could have been done more to make it every way convenient? <div eID="gen23244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23245" type="x-p"/> 2. How he entrusted these visible church-privileges with the nation and people of the Jews, especially their chief priests and elders; he let it out to them as husbandmen, not because he had need of them as landlords have of their tenants, but because he would try them, and be honoured by them. When in Judah God was known, and his name was great, when they were taken to be to God <hi type="italic">for a people, and for a name, and for a praise</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jer. xiii. 11</reference>), when he <hi type="italic">revealed his word unto Jacob</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.19">Ps. cxlvii. 19</reference>), when the <hi type="italic">covenant of life and peace</hi> was made with Levi (<reference osisRef="Mal.2.4-Mal.2.5">Mal. ii. 4, 5</reference>), then this vineyard was let out. See an abstract of the lease, <reference osisRef="Song.8.11-Song.8.12">Cant. viii. 11, 12</reference>. The Lord of the vineyard was to have <hi type="italic">a thousand pieces of silver</hi> (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.7.13">Isa. vii. 13</reference>); the main profit was to be his, but the keepers were to have two hundred, a competent and comfortable encouragement. And then he <hi type="italic">went into a far country.</hi> When God had in a visible appearance settled the Jewish church at mount Sinai, he did in a manner withdraw; they had no more such open vision, but were left to the written word. Or, they imagined that he was gone into a far country, as Israel, when they made the calf, fancied that Moses was gone. They put far from them the evil day. <div eID="gen23245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23246" type="x-p"/> II. God's expectation of rent from these husbandmen, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.34">v. 34</reference>. It was a reasonable expectation; for <hi type="italic">who plants a vineyard, and eats not of the fruit thereof?</hi> Note, From those that enjoy church-privileges, both ministers and people, God looks for fruit accordingly. 1. His expectations were not hasty; he did not demand a fore-rent, though he had been at such expense upon it; but staid <hi type="italic">till the time of the fruit drew near,</hi> as it did now that John preached the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven is at hand.</hi> God waits to be gracious, that he may give us time. 2. They were not high; he did not require them to come at their peril, upon penalty of forfeiting their lease if they ran behind-hand; but he sent his <hi type="italic">servants to them,</hi> to remind them of their duty, and of the rent-day, and to help them in gathering in the fruit, and making return of it. These servants were the prophets of the Old Testament, who were sent, and sometimes directly, to the people of the Jews, to reprove and instruct them. 3. They were not hard; it was only to <hi type="italic">receive the fruits.</hi> He did not demand more than they could make of it, but some fruit of that which he himself planted—an observance of the laws and statutes he gave them. What could have been done more reasonable? Israel was an empty vine, nay it was become the degenerate plant of a strange vine, and brought forth wild grapes. <div eID="gen23246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23247" type="x-p"/> III. The husbandmen's baseness in abusing the messengers that were sent to them. <div eID="gen23247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23248" type="x-p"/> 1. When he sent them his servants, they abused them, though they represented the master himself, and spoke in his name. Note, The calls and reproofs of the word, if they do not engage, will but exasperate. See here what hath all along been the lot of God's faithful messengers, more or less; (1.) To suffer; <hi type="italic">so persecuted they the prophets,</hi> who were hated with a cruel hatred. They not only despised and reproached them, but treated them as the worst of malefactors—they beat them, and killed them, and stoned them. They beat Jeremiah, killed Isaiah, stoned Zechariah the son of Jehoiada in the temple. If they that <hi type="italic">live godly in Christ Jesus</hi> themselves shall <hi type="italic">suffer persecution,</hi> much more they that press others to it. This was God's old quarrel with the Jews, misusing his prophets, <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.16">2 Chron. xxxvi. 16</reference>. (2.) It has been their lot to suffer from their Master's own tenants; they were the husbandmen that treated them thus, the chief priests and elders that <hi type="italic">sat in Moses's chair,</hi> that professed religion and relation to God; these were the most bitter enemies of the Lord's prophets, that cast them out, and killed them, and said, <hi type="italic">Let the Lord be glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.66.5">Isa. lxvi. 5</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Jer.20.1-Jer.20.2">Jer. xx. 1, 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.26.11">xxvi. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen23248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23249" type="x-p"/> Now see, [1.] How God persevered in his goodness to them. He sent other servants, more than the first; though the first sped not, but were abused. He had sent them John the Baptist, and him they had beheaded; and yet he sent them his disciples, to prepare his way. O the riches of the patience and forbearance of God, in keeping up in his church a despised, persecuted ministry! [2.] How they persisted in their wickedness. They <hi type="italic">did unto them likewise.</hi> One sin makes way for another of the same kind. They that are drunk with the blood of the saints, add drunkenness to thirst, and still cry, Give, give. <div eID="gen23249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23250" type="x-p"/> 2. At length, he sent them his Son; we have seen God's goodness in sending, and their badness in abusing, the servants; but in the latter instance both these exceed themselves. <div eID="gen23250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23251" type="x-p"/> (1.) Never did grace appear more gracious than in <hi type="italic">sending the Son.</hi> This was done <hi type="italic">last of all.</hi> Note, All the prophets were harbingers and forerunners to Christ. He was sent last; for if nothing else would work upon them, surely this would; it was therefore served for the <hi type="italic">ratio ultima—the last expedient. Surely they will reverence my Son,</hi> and therefore I will send him. Note, It might reasonably be expected that the Son of God, when he came to his own, should be reverenced; and reverence to Christ would be a powerful and effectual principle of fruitfulness and obedience, to the glory of God; if they will but reverence the Son, the point is gained. <hi type="italic">Surely they will reverence my Son,</hi> for he comes with more authority than the servants could; judgment is committed to him, that <hi type="italic">all men should honour him.</hi> There is greater danger in refusing him than in despising Moses's law. <div eID="gen23251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23252" type="x-p"/> (2.) Never did sin appear more sinful than in the abusing of him, which was now to be done in two or three days. Observe, <div eID="gen23252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23253" type="x-p"/> [1.] How it was plotted (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.38">v. 38</reference>); <hi type="italic">When they saw the Son:</hi> when he came, whom the people owned and followed as the Messiah, who would either have the rent paid, or distrain for it; this touched their copyhold, and they were resolved to make one bold push for it, and to preserve their wealth and grandeur by taking <hi type="italic">him</hi> out of the way, who was the only hindrance to it, and rival with them. <hi type="italic">This is the heir, come, let us kill him.</hi> Pilate and Herod, the princes of this world, <hi type="italic">knew not;</hi> for <hi type="italic">if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>. But the <hi type="italic">chief priests and elders</hi> knew that <hi type="italic">this was the heir,</hi> at least some of them; and therefore <hi type="italic">Come, let us kill him.</hi> Many are killed for what they have. The chief thing they envied him, and for which they hated and feared him, was his interest in the people, and their hosannas, which, if he was taken off, they hope to engross securely to themselves. They pretended that he must die, to save the people from the Romans (<reference osisRef="John.11.50">John xi. 50</reference>); but really he must die, to save their hypocrisy and tyranny from that reformation which the expected kingdom of the Messiah would certainly bring along with it. He drives the buyers and sellers out of the temple; and therefore <hi type="italic">let us kill him;</hi> and then, as if the premises must of course go to the occupant, <hi type="italic">let us seize on his inheritance.</hi> They thought, if they could but get rid of this Jesus, they should carry all before them in the church without control, might impose what traditions, and force the people to what submissions, they pleased. Thus they <hi type="italic">take counsel against the Lord and his Anointed;</hi> but he that <hi type="italic">sits in heaven,</hi> laughs to see them <hi type="italic">outshot in their own bow;</hi> for, while they thought to kill him, and so to seize on his inheritance, he went by his cross to his crown, and they were broken pieces with a rod of iron, and their inheritance seized. <reference osisRef="Ps.2.2-Ps.2.3">Ps. ii. 2, 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.9">9</reference>. <div eID="gen23253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23254" type="x-p"/> [2.] How this plot was executed, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.39">v. 39</reference>. While they were so set upon killing him, in pursuance of their design to secure their own pomp and power, and while he was so set upon dying, in pursuance of his design to subdue Satan, and save his chosen, no wonder if they soon <hi type="italic">caught him, and slew him,</hi> when his hour was come. Though the Roman power condemned him, yet it is still charged upon the chief priests and elders; for they were not only the prosecutors, but the principal agents, and had <hi type="italic">the greater sin. Ye have taken,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. Nay looking upon him to be as unworthy to live, as they were unwilling he should, <hi type="italic">they cast him out of the vineyard,</hi> out of the holy church, which they supposed themselves to have the key of, and out of the holy city for he was crucified <hi type="italic">without the gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.12">Heb. xiii. 12</reference>. As if <hi type="italic">He</hi> had been the shame and reproach, who was the greatest glory of his people Israel. Thus they who persecuted the servants, persecuted the Son; as men treat God's ministers, they would treat Christ himself, if he were with them. <div eID="gen23254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23255" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is their doom read out of their own mouths, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.40-Matt.21.41">v. 40, 41</reference>. He puts it to them, <hi type="italic">When the Lord of the vineyard cometh, what will he do unto these husbandmen?</hi> He puts it to themselves, for their stronger conviction, that <hi type="italic">knowing the judgment of God</hi> against them which do such things, they might be the more inexcusable. Note, God's proceedings are so unexceptionable, that there needs but an appeal to sinners themselves concerning the equity of them. God will be <hi type="italic">justified when he speaks.</hi> They could readily answer, <hi type="italic">He will miserably destroy those wicked men.</hi> Note, Many can easily prognosticate the dismal consequences of other people's sins, that see not what will be the end of their own. <div eID="gen23255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23256" type="x-p"/> 1. Our Saviour, in his question, supposes that <hi type="italic">the lord of the vineyard will come,</hi> and reckon with them. God is the Lord of the vineyard; the property is his, and he will make <hi type="italic">them</hi> know it, who now <hi type="italic">lord it over his heritage,</hi> as if it were all their own. The Lord of the vineyard will come. Persecutors say in their hearts, He <hi type="italic">delays his coming,</hi> he <hi type="italic">doth not see,</hi> he <hi type="italic">will not require;</hi> but they shall find, though he bear long with them, he will not bear always. It is comfort to abused saints and ministers, that <hi type="italic">the Lord is at hand,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Judge stands before the door.</hi> When he comes, what will he do to carnal professors? What will he do to cruel persecutors? They must be called to account, they have their day now; but he <hi type="italic">sees that his day is coming.</hi> <div eID="gen23256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23257" type="x-p"/> 2. They, in their answer, suppose that it will be a terrible reckoning; the crime appearing so very black, you may be sure, <div eID="gen23257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23258" type="x-p"/> (1.) That he will <hi type="italic">miserably destroy those wicked men;</hi> it is destruction that is their doom. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Kakous kakos apolesei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Malos male perdet.</hi> Let men never expect to do ill, and fare well. This was fulfilled upon the Jews, in that miserable destruction which was brought upon them by the Romans, and was completed about forty years after this; and unparalleled ruin, attended with all the most dismal aggravating circumstances. It will be fulfilled upon all that tread in the steps of their wickedness; hell is everlasting destruction, and it will be the most miserable destruction to them of all others, that have enjoyed the greatest share of church privileges, and have not improved them. The hottest place in hell will be the portion of hypocrites and persecutors. <div eID="gen23258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23259" type="x-p"/> (2.) That he will <hi type="italic">let out his vineyard to other husbandmen.</hi> Note, God will have a church in the world, notwithstanding the unworthiness and opposition of many that abuse the privileges of it. The unbelief and frowardness of man shall not make the word of God of no effect. If one will not, another will. The Jews' leavings were the Gentiles' feast. Persecutors may destroy the ministers, but cannot destroy the church. The Jews imagined that no doubt <hi type="italic">they were the people,</hi> and wisdom and holiness must <hi type="italic">die with them;</hi> and if they were cut off, what would God do for a church in the world? But when God makes use of any to bear up his name, it is not because he needs them, nor is he at all beholden to them. If we were made a desolation and an astonishment, God could build a flourishing church upon our ruins; for he is never at a loss what to do for his great name, whatever becomes of us, and of our place and nation. <div eID="gen23259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23260" type="x-p"/> V. The further illustration and application of this by Christ himself, telling them, in effect, that they had rightly judged. <div eID="gen23260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23261" type="x-p"/> 1. He illustrates it by referring to a scripture fulfilled in this (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.42">v. 42</reference>); <hi type="italic">Did ye never read in the scriptures?</hi> Yes, no doubt, they had often read and sung it, but had not considered it. We lose the benefit of what we read for want of meditation. The scripture he quotes is <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22-Ps.118.23">Ps. cxviii. 22, 23</reference>, the same context out of which the children fetched their hosannas. The same word yields matter of praise and comfort to Christ's friends and followers, which speaks conviction and terror to his enemies. Such a two-edged sword is the word of God. That scripture, the <hi type="italic">Stone which the builders refused is become the headstone of the corner,</hi> illustrates the preceding parable, especially that part of it which refers to Christ. <div eID="gen23261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23262" type="x-p"/> (1.) The builders' rejecting of the stone is the same with the husbandmen's abusing of the son that was sent to them. The chief priests and the elders were the builders, had the oversight of the Jewish church, which was God's building: and they would not allow Christ a place in their building, would not admit his doctrine or laws into their constitution; they threw him aside as a despised broken vessel, a stone that would serve only for a stepping-stone, to be trampled upon. <div eID="gen23262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23263" type="x-p"/> (2.) The advancing of this stone to be the head of the corner is the same with <hi type="italic">letting out the vineyard to other husbandmen.</hi> He who was rejected by the Jews was embraced by the Gentiles; and to that church where there is no difference of circumcision or uncircumcision, <hi type="italic">Christ is all, and in all.</hi> His authority over the gospel church, and influence upon it, his ruling it as the Head, and uniting it as the Corner-stone, are the great tokens of his exhaltation. Thus, in spite of the malice of the priests and elders, he <hi type="italic">divided a portion with the great,</hi> and received <hi type="italic">his kingdom,</hi> though they would not have him to reign over them. <div eID="gen23263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23264" type="x-p"/> (3.) The hand of God was in all this; <hi type="italic">This is the Lord's doing.</hi> Even the rejecting of him by the Jewish builders was by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God; he permitted and overruled it; much more was his advancement to the Head of the corner; his right hand and his holy arm brought it about; it was God himself that <hi type="italic">highly exalted him,</hi> and gave him <hi type="italic">a name above every name; and it is marvellous in our eyes.</hi> The wickedness of the Jews that rejected him is marvellous; that men should be so prejudiced against their own interest! See <reference osisRef="Isa.29.9-Isa.29.10">Isa. xxix. 9, 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.14">14</reference>. The honour done him by the Gentile world, notwithstanding the abuses done him by his own people, is marvellous; that he whom men despised and abhorred, should be adored by kings! <reference osisRef="Isa.49.7">Isa. xlix. 7</reference>. But <hi type="italic">it is the Lord's doing.</hi> <div eID="gen23264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23265" type="x-p"/> 2. He applies it to them, and application is the life of preaching. <div eID="gen23265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23266" type="x-p"/> (1.) He applies the sentence which they had passed (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.41">v. 41</reference>), and turns it upon themselves; not the former part of it, concerning the miserable destruction of the husbandmen (he could not bear to speak of that), but the latter part, of <hi type="italic">letting out the vineyard to others;</hi> because though it looked black upon the Jews, it spoke good to the Gentiles. Know then, <div eID="gen23266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23267" type="x-p"/> [1.] That the Jews shall be unchurched; <hi type="italic">The kingdom of God shall be taken from you.</hi> This turning out of the husbandmen speaks the same doom with that of dismantling the vineyard, and laying it common. <reference osisRef="Isa.5.5">Isa. v. 5</reference>. To the Jews had long pertained <hi type="italic">the adoption and the glory</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>); to them were committed the <hi type="italic">oracles of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.2">Rom. iii. 2</reference>), and the sacred trust of revealed religion, and bearing up of God's name in the world (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.2">Ps. lxxvi. 1, 2</reference>); but now it shall be so no longer. They were not only unfruitful in the use of their privileges, but, under pretence of them, opposed the gospel of Christ, and so forfeited them, and it was not long ere the forfeiture was taken. Note, It is a righteous thing with God to remove church privileges from those that not only sin against them, but sin with them, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.4-Rev.2.5">Rev. ii. 4, 5</reference>. The kingdom of God was taken from the Jews, not only by the temporal judgments that befel them, but by the spiritual judgments they lay under, their blindness of mind, hardness of heart, and indignation at the gospel, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.8-Rom.11.10">Rom. xi. 8-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15">1 Thess. ii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen23267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23268" type="x-p"/> [2.] That the Gentiles shall be taken in. God needs not ask us leave whether he shall have a church in the world; though his vine be plucked up in one place, he will find another to plant it in. He will give it <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ethnei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to the Gentile world,</hi> that will <hi type="italic">bring forth the fruit of it.</hi> They who had been not a people, and had not obtained mercy, became favourites of Heaven. This is the mystery which blessed Paul was so much affected with (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.30">Rom. xi. 30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">33</reference>), and which the Jews were so much affronted by, <reference osisRef="Acts.22.21-Acts.22.22">Acts xxii. 21, 22</reference>. At the first planting of Israel in Canaan, the <hi type="italic">fall of the Gentiles was the riches of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.10-Ps.135.11">Ps. cxxxv. 10, 11</reference>), so, at their extirpation, the fall of Israel was the riches of the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.12">Rom. xi. 12</reference>. It shall go to <hi type="italic">a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof.</hi> Note, Christ knows beforehand who will bring forth gospel fruits in the use of gospel means; because our fruitfulness is all the work of his own hands, and <hi type="italic">known unto God are all his works.</hi> They shall bring forth the fruits better than the Jews had done; God has had more glory from the New Testament church than from that of the Old Testament; for, when he changes, it shall not be to his loss. <div eID="gen23268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23269" type="x-p"/> (2.) He applies the scripture which he had quoted (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.42">v. 42</reference>), to their terror, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">v. 44</reference>. This <hi type="italic">Stone,</hi> which the <hi type="italic">builders refused, is set for the fall of many in Israel;</hi> and we have here the doom of two sorts of people, for whose fall it proves that Christ is set. <div eID="gen23269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23270" type="x-p"/> [1.] Some, through ignorance, stumble at Christ in his estate of humiliation; when this Stone lies on the earth, where the builders threw it, they, through their blindness and carelessness, fall on it, fall over it, and <hi type="italic">they shall be broken.</hi> The offence they take at Christ, will not hurt him, any more than he that stumbles, hurts the stone he stumbles at; but it will hurt themselves; they will fall, and be broken, and snared, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.14">Isa. viii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.7-1Pet.2.8">1 Pet. ii. 7, 8</reference>. The unbelief of sinners will be their ruin. <div eID="gen23270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23271" type="x-p"/> [2.] Others, through malice, oppose Christ, and bid defiance to him in his estate of exaltation, when this Stone is advanced to the head of the corner; and on them <hi type="italic">it shall fall,</hi> for they pull it on their own heads, as the Jews did by that challenge, <hi type="italic">His blood be upon us and upon our children,</hi> and <hi type="italic">it will grind them to powder.</hi> The former seems to bespeak the sin and ruin of all unbelievers; this is the greater sin, and sorer ruin, of persecutors, that <hi type="italic">kick against the pricks,</hi> and persist in it. Christ's kingdom will be a burthensome stone to all those that attempt to overthrow it, or heave it out of its place; see <reference osisRef="Zech.12.3">Zech. xii. 3</reference>. This Stone cut out of the mountain without hands, will break in pieces all opposing power, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.34-Dan.2.35">Dan. ii. 34, 35</reference>. Some make this an allusion to the manner of stoning to death among the Jews. The malefactors were first thrown down violently from a high scaffold upon a great stone, which would much bruise them; but then they threw another great stone upon them, which would crush them to pieces: one way or other, Christ will utterly destroy all those that fight against him. If they be so stout-hearted, that they are not destroyed by falling on this stone, yet it shall fall on them, and so destroy them. He will <hi type="italic">strike through kings,</hi> he will <hi type="italic">fill the places with dead bodies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.5-Ps.110.6">Ps. cx. 5, 6</reference>. None ever hardened his heart against God and prospered. <div eID="gen23271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23272" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The entertainment which this discourse of Christ met with among the chief priests and elders, that heard his parables. <div eID="gen23272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23273" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">They perceived that he spake of them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.25">v. 45</reference>), and that in what they said (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.41">v. 41</reference>) they had but read their own doom. Note, A guilty conscience needs no accuser, and sometimes will save a minister the labour of saying, <hi type="italic">Thou art the man. Mutato nomine, de te fabula narratur—Change but the name, the tale is told of the.</hi> So quick and powerful is the word of God, and such a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart, that it is easy for bad men (if conscience be not quite seared) to perceive that it speaks of them. <div eID="gen23273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23274" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">They sought to lay hands on him.</hi> Note, When those who hear the reproofs of the word, perceive that it speaks of them, if it do not do them a great deal of good, it will certainly do them a great deal of hurt. If they be not pricked to the heart with conviction and contrition, as they were <reference osisRef="Acts.2.37">Acts ii. 37</reference>, they will be cut to the heart with rage and indignation, as they were <reference osisRef="Acts.5.33">Acts v. 33</reference>. <div eID="gen23274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23275" type="x-p"/> 3. They durst not do it, <hi type="italic">for fear of the multitude, who took him for a prophet,</hi> though not for the Messiah; this served to keep the Pharisees in awe. The fear of the people restrained them from speaking ill of John (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.26">v. 26</reference>), and here from doing ill to Christ. Note, God has many ways of restraining the remainders of wrath, as he has of making that which breaks out redound to his praise, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.10">Ps. lxxvi. 10</reference>.  <chapter eID="Matt.21"/> <div eID="gen23275" type="x-p"/>

entries.d859109d0a334a61db5f055debae70186300b120: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13719"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 21</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.21.1-Matt.21.9">Mt 21:1-9</reference>. Christ's Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem on the First Day of the Week. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.11.1-Mark.11.11">Mr 11:1-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.29-Luke.19.40">Lu 19:29-40</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.12-John.12.19">Joh 12:12-19</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26307" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For the exposition of this majestic scene--</hi>recorded, as will be seen, by all the Evangelists--see on <reference osisRef="Luke.19.29-Luke.19.40">Lu 19:29-40</reference>.<div eID="gen26307" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.21.10-Matt.21.22">Mt 21:10-22</reference>. Stir about Him in the City--Second Cleansing of the Temple, and Miracles There--Glorious Vindication of the Children's Testimony--The Barren Fig Tree Cursed, with Lessons from It. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.11.11-Mark.11.26">Mr 11:11-26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.45-Luke.19.48">Lu 19:45-48</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26308" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Luke.19.45-Luke.19.48">Lu 19:45-48</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Mark.11.12-Mark.11.26">Mr 11:12-26</reference>.<div eID="gen26308" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.21.23-Matt.21.46">Mt 21:23-46</reference>. The Authority of Jesus Questioned and the Reply--The Parables of the Two Sons, and of the Wicked Husbandman. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.11.27-Mark.12.12">Mr 11:27-12:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.20.1-Luke.20.19">Lu 20:1-19</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26309" type="x-p"/> Now commences, as Alford remarks, that series of parables and discourses of our Lord with His enemies, in which He develops, more completely than ever before, His hostility to their hypocrisy and iniquity: and so they are stirred up to compass His death.<div eID="gen26309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26310" type="x-p"/> The Authority of Jesus Questioned, and the Reply (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.23-Matt.21.27">Mt 21:23-27</reference>).<div eID="gen26310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26311" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13719"/><hi type="bold">23. By what authority doest thou these things!--</hi>referring particularly to the expulsion of the buyers and sellers from the temple,<div eID="gen26311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26312" type="x-p"/> and who gave thee this authority? <div eID="gen26312" type="x-p"/>
entries.466f2ba22dc424978896882a099392e8b21f3f36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13720"/><div sID="gen26313" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13720"/>24. And Jesus answered and said unto them, I also will ask you one thing, &c. <div eID="gen26313" type="x-p"/>
entries.ceed8bbb8b382ecd0362d99dafbc4523bf19e813: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13721"/><div sID="gen26314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13721"/><hi type="bold">25. The baptism of John--</hi>meaning his whole mission and ministry, of which baptism was the proper character.<div eID="gen26314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whence was it? from heaven, or of men?--</hi>What wisdom there was in this way of meeting their question will best appear by their reply.<div eID="gen26315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">If we shall say, From heaven; he will say unto us, Why did ye not then believe him?--</hi>"Why did ye not believe the testimony which he bore to Me, as the promised and expected Messiah?" for that was the burden of John's whole testimony. <div eID="gen26316" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9c1a1ee2b85c87851e9f4784a27273d832e6ac3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13722"/><div sID="gen26317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13722"/><hi type="bold">26. But if we shall say, Of men; we fear the people--</hi>rather, "the multitude." In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.6">Lu 20:6</reference>) it is, "all the people will stone us"--"stone us to death."<div eID="gen26317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for all hold John as a prophet--</hi>Crooked, cringing hypocrites! No wonder Jesus gave you no answer. <div eID="gen26318" type="x-p"/>
entries.15c897961001118b1b57a7b699255853745f6c8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13723"/><div sID="gen26319" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13723"/><hi type="bold">27. And they answered Jesus, and said, We cannot tell--</hi>Evidently their difficulty was, how to answer, so as neither to shake their determination to reject the claims of Christ nor damage their reputation with the people. For the truth itself they cared nothing whatever.<div eID="gen26319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Neither tell I you by what authority I do these things--</hi>What composure and dignity of wisdom does our Lord here display, as He turns their question upon themselves, and, while revealing His knowledge of their hypocrisy, closes their mouths! Taking advantage of the surprise, silence, and awe produced by this reply, our Lord followed it up immediately by the two following parables.<div eID="gen26320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26321" type="x-p"/> Parable of the Two Sons (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.28-Matt.21.32">Mt 21:28-32</reference>). <div eID="gen26321" type="x-p"/>
entries.e118f98f66b2f99f01b44d9380924a7f9b11b7e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13724"/><div sID="gen26322" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13724"/><hi type="bold">28. But what think ye? A certain man had two sons; and he came to the first and said, Son, go work to-day in my vineyard--</hi>for true religion is a practical thing, a "bringing forth fruit unto God." <div eID="gen26322" type="x-p"/>
entries.206f0b6ed7167ce6a2111ed3d2cb781a112a5d65: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13725"/><div sID="gen26323" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13725"/><hi type="bold">29. He answered and said, I will not--</hi>Trench notices the rudeness of this answer, and the total absence of any attempt to excuse such disobedience, both characteristic; representing careless, reckless sinners resisting God to His face. <div eID="gen26323" type="x-p"/>
entries.e36875fcd6ff8dca668d14d5752eb653df15c01e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13726"/><div sID="gen26324" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13726"/><hi type="bold">30. And he came to the second, and said likewise. And he answered and said, I go, sir--</hi>"I, sir." The emphatic "I," here, denotes the self-righteous complacency which says, "God, I thank thee that I am not as other men" (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.11">Lu 18:11</reference>).<div eID="gen26324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26325" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and went not--</hi>He did not "afterward repent" and refuse to go; for there was here no intention to go. It is the class that "say and do not" (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.3">Mt 23:3</reference>)--a falseness more abominable to God, says Stier, than any "I will not." <div eID="gen26325" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd6c8d45108f462287a7a20ba667af3d67bd74bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13727"/><div sID="gen26326" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13727"/><hi type="bold">31. Whether of them twain did the will of his Father? They say unto him, The first--</hi>Now comes the application.<div eID="gen26326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26327" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go--</hi>or, "are going"; even now entering, while ye hold back.<div eID="gen26327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into the kingdom of God before you--</hi>The publicans and the harlots were the first son, who, when told to work in the Lord's vineyard, said, I will not; but afterwards repented and went. Their early life was a flat and flagrant refusal to do what they were commanded; it was one continued rebellion against the authority of God. The chief priests and the elders of the people, with whom our Lord was now speaking, were the second son, who said, I go, sir, but went not. They were early called, and all their life long professed obedience to God, but never rendered it; their life was one of continued disobedience. <div eID="gen26328" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe7dadd8a14327244447e071619a66f5f69c1708: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13728"/><div sID="gen26329" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13728"/><hi type="bold">32. For John came unto you in the way of righteousness--</hi>that is, calling you to repentance; as Noah is styled "a preacher of righteousness" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.5">2Pe 2:5</reference>), when like the Baptist he warned the old world to "flee from the wrath to come."<div eID="gen26329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and ye believed him not--</hi>They did not reject him; nay, they "were willing for a season to rejoice in his light" (<reference osisRef="John.5.35">Joh 5:35</reference>); but they would not receive his testimony to Jesus.<div eID="gen26330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26331" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but the publicans and the harlots believed him--</hi>Of the publicans this is twice expressly recorded, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.12">Lu 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.7.29">7:29</reference>. Of the harlots, then, the same may be taken for granted, though the fact is not expressly recorded. These outcasts gladly believed the testimony of John to the coming Saviour, and so hastened to Jesus when He came. See <reference osisRef="Luke.7.37">Lu 7:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.15.1">15:1</reference>, &c.<div eID="gen26331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26332" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and ye, when ye had seen it, repented not afterward, that ye might believe him--</hi>Instead of being "provoked to jealousy" by their example, ye have seen them flocking to the Saviour and getting to heaven, unmoved.<div eID="gen26332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26333" type="x-p"/> Parable of the Wicked Husbandmen (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.33-Matt.21.46">Mt 21:33-46</reference>). <div eID="gen26333" type="x-p"/>
entries.375cfe4b94f6b4d833dfcc7a6c4e3b0036e82c76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13729"/><div sID="gen26334" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13729"/><hi type="bold">33. Hear another parable: There was a certain householder, which planted a vineyard--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Luke.13.6">Lu 13:6</reference>).<div eID="gen26334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26335" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and hedged it round about, and digged a winepress in it, and built a tower--</hi>These details are taken, as is the basis of the parable itself, from that beautiful parable of <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1-Isa.5.7">Is 5:1-7</reference>, in order to fix down the application and sustain it by Old Testament authority.<div eID="gen26335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and let it out to husbandmen--</hi>These are just the ordinary spiritual guides of the people, under whose care and culture the fruits of righteousness are expected to spring up.<div eID="gen26336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26337" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and went into a far country--</hi>"for a long time" (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.9">Lu 20:9</reference>), leaving the vineyard to the laws of the spiritual husbandry during the whole time of the Jewish economy. On this phraseology, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.4.26">Mr 4:26</reference>. <div eID="gen26337" type="x-p"/>
entries.a939e6d87f5d62bc2d17f58f6aa73c44a686ff1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13730"/><div sID="gen26338" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13730"/><hi type="bold">34. And when the time of the fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the husbandmen--</hi>By these "servants" are meant the prophets and other extraordinary messengers, raised up from time to time. See on <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Mt 23:37</reference>.<div eID="gen26338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they might receive the fruits of it--</hi>Again see on <reference osisRef="Luke.13.6">Lu 13:6</reference>. <div eID="gen26339" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb11000024d425800f1fffa50a8f6a399356d587: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13731"/><div sID="gen26340" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13731"/><hi type="bold">35. And the husbandmen took his servants, and beat one--</hi>see <reference osisRef="Jer.37.15">Jr 37:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.6">38:6</reference>.<div eID="gen26340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26341" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and killed another--</hi>see <reference osisRef="Jer.26.20-Jer.26.23">Jr 26:20-23</reference>.<div eID="gen26341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and stoned another--</hi>see <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.21">2Ch 24:21</reference>. Compare with this whole verse <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Mt 23:37</reference>, where our Lord reiterates these charges in the most melting strain. <div eID="gen26342" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1c400ad7ce8be0576e4b1b636b1b2cdcb6eeae5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13732"/><div sID="gen26343" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13732"/><hi type="bold">36. Again, he sent other servants more than the first; and they did unto them likewise--</hi>see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.13">2Ki 17:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.16">2Ch 36:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.26">Ne 9:26</reference>. <div eID="gen26343" type="x-p"/>
entries.d6437e978943f50ed85f1e461e7dce557f390590: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13733"/><div sID="gen26344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13733"/><hi type="bold">37. But last of all he sent unto them his son, saying, They will reverence my son--</hi>In Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.6">Mr 12:6</reference>) this is most touchingly expressed: "Having yet therefore one son, His well-beloved, He sent Him also last unto them, saying, They will reverence My Son." Luke's version of it too (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.13">Lu 20:13</reference>) is striking: "Then said the lord of the vineyard, What shall I do? I will send My beloved Son: it may be they will reverence Him when they see Him." Who does not see that our Lord here severs Himself, by the sharpest line of demarcation, from all merely human messengers, and claims for Himself Sonship in its loftiest sense? (Compare <reference osisRef="Heb.3.3-Heb.3.6">He 3:3-6</reference>). The expression, "It may be they will reverence My Son," is designed to teach the almost unimaginable guilt of not reverentially welcoming God's Son. <div eID="gen26344" type="x-p"/>
entries.21536c83018ff78993e4ac5a08fc29145461018c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13734"/><div sID="gen26345" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13734"/><hi type="bold">38. But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.37.18-Gen.37.20">Ge 37:18-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.11.47-John.11.53">Joh 11:47-53</reference>.<div eID="gen26345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">This is the heir--</hi>Sublime expression this of the great truth, that God's inheritance was destined for, and in due time is to come into the possession of, His own Son in our nature (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">He 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen26346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance--</hi>that so, from mere servants, we may become lords. This is the deep aim of the depraved heart; this is emphatically "the root of all evil." <div eID="gen26347" type="x-p"/>
entries.a97724cf7695528490f74c2a9351827d523df0ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13735"/><div sID="gen26348" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13735"/><hi type="bold">39. And they caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard--</hi>compare <reference osisRef="Heb.13.11-Heb.13.13">He 13:11-13</reference> ("without the gate--without the camp"); <reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.13">1Ki 21:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.19.17">Joh 19:17</reference>.<div eID="gen26348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26349" type="x-p"/> and slew him. <div eID="gen26349" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd0eeac4478e07c552b78f55321f69ddc95c7750: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13736"/><div sID="gen26350" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13736"/><hi type="bold">40. When the lord therefore of the vineyard cometh--</hi>This represents "the settling time," which, in the case of the Jewish ecclesiastics, was that judicial trial of the nation and its leaders which issued in the destruction of their whole state.<div eID="gen26350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26351" type="x-p"/> what will he do unto those husbandmen? <div eID="gen26351" type="x-p"/>
entries.94bbabf8a0bc8c5f7b15be83964a7ce4d480d235: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13737"/><div sID="gen26352" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13737"/><hi type="bold">41. They say unto him, He will miserably destroy those wicked men--</hi>an emphatic alliteration not easily conveyed in English: "He will badly destroy those bad men," or "miserably destroy those miserable men," is something like it.<div eID="gen26352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and will let out his vineyard unto other husbandmen, which shall render him the fruits in their seasons--</hi>If this answer was given by the Pharisees, to whom our Lord addressed the parable, they thus unwittingly pronounced their own condemnation: as did David to Nathan the prophet (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.5-2Sam.12.7">2Sa 12:5-7</reference>), and Simon the Pharisee to our Lord (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.43">Lu 7:43</reference>, &c.). But if it was given, as the two other Evangelists agree in representing it, by our Lord Himself, and the explicitness of the answer would seem to favor that supposition, then we can better explain the exclamation of the Pharisees which followed it, in Luke's report (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.16">Lu 20:16</reference>)--"And when they heard it, they said, God forbid"--His whole meaning now bursting upon them. <div eID="gen26353" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4fd7f4e0dd8f098b31972f3d40495e279feca61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13738"/><div sID="gen26354" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13738"/><hi type="bold">42. Jesus saith unto them. Did ye never read in the scriptures--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.118.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen26354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26355" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The stone which the builders rejected, &c.--</hi>A bright Messianic prophecy, which reappears in various forms (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>, &c.), and was made glorious use of by Peter before the Sanhedrim (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.11">Ac 4:11</reference>). He recurs to it in his first epistle (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.4-1Pet.2.6">1Pe 2:4-6</reference>). <div eID="gen26355" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3fb3107bc17530b350299cf22bf4e8ea7ef8119: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13739"/><div sID="gen26356" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13739"/><hi type="bold">43. Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God--</hi>God's visible Kingdom, or Church, upon earth, which up to this time stood in the seed of Abraham.<div eID="gen26356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof--</hi>that is, the great evangelical community of the faithful, which, after the extrusion of the Jewish nation, would consist chiefly of Gentiles, until "all Israel should be saved" (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.25">Ro 11:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">26</reference>). This vastly important statement is given by Matthew only. <div eID="gen26357" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c88a4657e0065df1b8ba30d928184297e15996f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13740"/><div sID="gen26358" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13740"/><hi type="bold">44. And whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder--</hi>The Kingdom of God is here a Temple, in the erection of which a certain stone, rejected as unsuitable by the spiritual builders, is, by the great Lord of the House, made the keystone of the whole. On that Stone the builders were now "falling" and being "broken" (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.15">Is 8:15</reference>). They were sustaining great spiritual hurt; but soon that Stone should "fall upon them" and "grind them to powder" (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.34">Da 2:34</reference>, 35; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.2">Zec 12:2</reference>)--in their corporate capacity, in the tremendous destruction of Jerusalem, but personally, as unbelievers, in a more awful sense still. <div eID="gen26358" type="x-p"/>
entries.22ce7e0c9d637abd1141fb370dc1262550cb94dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13741"/><div sID="gen26359" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13741"/><hi type="bold">45. And when the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables--</hi>referring to that of the Two Sons and this one of the Wicked Husbandmen.<div eID="gen26359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26360" type="x-p"/> they perceived that he spake of them. <div eID="gen26360" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0dbd8b2b5327d1fdc31b1e82920cb32e80c1851: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13742"/><div sID="gen26361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13742"/><hi type="bold">46. But when they sought to lay hands on him--</hi>which Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.19">Lu 20:19</reference>) says they did "the same hour," hardly able to restrain their rage.<div eID="gen26361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they feared the multitude--</hi>rather, "the multitudes."<div eID="gen26362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because they took him for a prophet--</hi>just as they feared to say John's baptism was of men, because the masses took him for a prophet (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.26">Mt 21:26</reference>). Miserable creatures! So, for this time, "they left Him and went their way" (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.12">Mr 12:12</reference>). <chapter eID="Matt.21"/>

entries.88494f284388af4275df8cce89481b8573226ff4: <div eID="gen38004" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen38005" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen38006" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen38006" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen38005" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen38007" type="x-p"/> Christ rides into Jerusalem upon an ass, and the multitude receive him joyfully, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.1-Mat.21.11">Mat 21:1-11</reference>. He enters the temple, and expels the money-changers, etc. <reference osisRef="Mat.21.12">Mat 21:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.13">Mat 21:13</reference>. The blind and the lame come to him and are healed, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.14">Mat 21:14</reference>. The chief priests and scribes are offended, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.15">Mat 21:15</reference>. Our Lord confounds them, and goes to Bethany, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.16">Mat 21:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.17">Mat 21:17</reference>. The barren fig-tree blasted, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.18-Mat.21.22">Mat 21:18-22</reference>. While teaching in the temple, the chief priests and elders question his authority; he answers and confutes them, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.23-Mat.21.27">Mat 21:23-27</reference>. The parable of the man and his two sons, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.28-Mat.21.32">Mat 21:28-32</reference>. The parable of a vineyard let out to husbandmen, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.33-Mat.21.42">Mat 21:33-42</reference>; applied to the priests and Pharisees, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.43-Mat.21.45">Mat 21:43-45</reference>; who wish to kill him, but are restrained by the fear of the people, who acknowledge Christ for a prophet, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.46">Mat 21:46</reference>. <div eID="gen38007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38008" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen38008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38009" type="x-p"/> Bethphage - A place on the west declivity of Mount Olivet, from which it is thought the whole declivity and part of the valley took their name. It is supposed to have derived its name from the fig-trees which grew there; בית beeth, signifying a region as well as a house, and פג phag, a green fig.
entries.41097f0f2d24c2ad7547293d251527c0d8058d54: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen38009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38010" type="x-p"/> Ye shall find an ass tied, and a colt - Asses and mules were in common use in Palestine: horses were seldom to be met with. Our blessed Lord takes every opportunity to convince his disciples that nothing was hidden from him: he informs them of the most minute occurrence; and manifested his power over the heart in disposing the owner to permit the ass to be taken away.
entries.b467e771952f167d3d2a0d6096771a3f7df2d034: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen38010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38011" type="x-p"/> The Lord (the proprietor of all things) hath need of them - Jesus is continually humbling himself, to show us how odious pride is in the sight of God: but in his humility he is ever giving proofs of his almighty power, that the belief of his divinity may be established.
entries.62f697b8eea655ce65cd008fdfcbdd43ffe0857f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen38011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38012" type="x-p"/> All this was done - The word all, in this clause, is omitted by some MSS., versions, and fathers. <div eID="gen38012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38013" type="x-p"/> Which was spoken - The Spirit of God, which predicted those things that concerned the Messiah, took care to have them literally fulfilled: <div eID="gen38013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38014" type="x-p"/> 1. To show the truth of prophecy in general; and, <div eID="gen38014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38015" type="x-p"/> 2. To designate Christ as the person intended by that prophecy. <div eID="gen38015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38016" type="x-p"/> See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.2.23">Mat 2:23</reference>.
entries.38047be55a29617bbf9c05d26ae6572d45b09d18: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen38016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38017" type="x-p"/> Tell ye the daughter of Sion - The quotation is taken from <reference osisRef="Zac.9.9">Zac 9:9</reference>, but not in the precise words of the prophet. <div eID="gen38017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38018" type="x-p"/> This entry into Jerusalem has been termed the triumph of Christ. It was indeed the triumph of humility over pride and worldly grandeur; of poverty over affluence; and of meekness and gentleness over rage and malice. <div eID="gen38018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38019" type="x-p"/> He is coming now meek, full of kindness and compassion to those who were plotting his destruction! He comes to deliver up himself into their hands; their king comes to be murdered by his subjects, and to make his death a ransom price for their souls!
entries.93ec12f3aaf5039ca2fcfff97e3bc977aab1983e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen38019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38020" type="x-p"/> And put on them their clothes - Thus acknowledging him to be their king, for this was a custom observed by the people when they found that God had appointed a man to the kingdom. When Jehu sat with the captains of the army, and Elisha the prophet came, by the order of God, to anoint him king over Israel, as soon as he came out of the inner chamber into which the prophet had taken him to anoint him, and they knew what was done, every man took his garment, and spread it under him on the top of the steps, and blew the trumpets, saying, "Jehu is king." <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.13">2Kgs 9:13</reference>. <div eID="gen38020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38021" type="x-p"/> And they set him thereon - Και επεκαθισεν επανω αυτων, and he sat upon them; but instead of επανω αυτων, upon Them, the Codex Bezae, seven copies of the Itala, some copies of the Vulgate, and some others, read επ' αυτον, upon him, i.e. the colt. This is most likely to be the true reading; for we can scarcely suppose that he rode upon both by turns, - this would appear childish; or that he rode upon both at once, for this would be absurd. Some say he sat on both; for "the ass that was tied up was an emblem of the Jews bound under the yoke of the law; and the colt that had not been tied represented the Gentiles who were not under the law; and that Jesus Christ's sitting on both represented his subjecting the Jews and the Gentiles to the sway of his evangelical scepter." He who can receive this saying, let him receive it.
entries.c0b2f62111908e18ed7f98acd30dc62d9f8751a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen38021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38022" type="x-p"/> Cut down branches from the trees - Carrying palm and other branches was emblematical of victory and success. See 1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7; and <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev 7:9</reference>. <div eID="gen38022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38023" type="x-p"/> The rabbins acknowledge that the prophecy in Zechariah refers to the Messiah; so Rab. Tancum, and Yalcut Rubeni has a strange story about the ass. "This ass is the colt of that ass which was created in the twilight of the sixth day. This is the ass which Abraham found when he went to sacrifice his son. This is the ass on which Moses rode when he went to Egypt; and this is the ass on which the Messiah shall ride." Some of the Jews seem to think that the zebra is intended; for according to Bab. Sanhedr. fol. 98, when Shapoor, king of Persia, said to Rabbi Samuel: "You say your Messiah will come upon an ass; I will send him a noble horse." To which the rabbi replied, "You have not a horse with a hundred spots (query, streaks) like his ass." See Lightfoot and Schoettgen.
entries.a8762a868ebd7baddaf92371bff54c6534926b3c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen38023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38024" type="x-p"/> Hosanna to the son of David - When persons applied to the king for help, or for a redress of grievances, they used the word hosanna, or rather from the Hebrew הושיעה נא Hoshiah Na! Save now! or, Save, we beseech thee! - redress our grievances, and give us help from oppression! Thus both the words and actions of the people prove that they acknowledged Christ as their king, and looked to him for deliverance. How easily might he have assumed the sovereignty at this time, had he been so disposed! For instances of the use of this form of speech, see <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.4">2Sam 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.26">2Kgs 6:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.118.25">Psa 118:25</reference>. <div eID="gen38024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38025" type="x-p"/> Son of David - A well-known epithet of the Messiah. He who cometh in the name, etc. He who comes in the name and authority of the Most High. <div eID="gen38025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38026" type="x-p"/> Hosanna in the highest - Either meaning, Let the heavenly hosts join with us in magnifying this august Being! - or, Let the utmost degrees of hosanna, of salvation, and deliverance, be communicated to thy people! Probably there is an allusion here to the custom of the Jews in the feast of tabernacles. During the first seven days of that feast, they went once round the altar, each day, with palm and other branches in their hands, singing Hosanna: but on the eighth day of that feast they walked seven times round the altar, singing the hosanna; and this was termed the hosanna rabba, the Great hosanna: i.e. Assist with the greatest succor. Probably answering to the τοις υψιστοις of the evangelist, for on this day they beg the most speedy and powerful help against their enemies, and likewise pray for a prosperous and fruitful year. See Stehlin's Jewish Traditions, vol. ii. p. 322.
entries.6c9beae614421343df2662f27a3f5058cd985310: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen38026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38027" type="x-p"/> All the city was moved - Or, the whole city was in motion. Εσεισθη, was in a tumult - they saw and heard plainly that the multitude had proclaimed Christ king, and Messiah. Who is this? Who is accounted worthy of this honor?
entries.e25a1b869f2ebaafa7717e398f28ab295c82a5ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen38027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38028" type="x-p"/> This is Jesus The Prophet - Ο προφητης That prophet whom Moses spoke of, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.18">Deu 18:18</reference>. I will raise them up a prophet - like unto thee, etc. Every expression of the multitude plainly intimated that they fully received our blessed Lord as the promised Messiah. - How strange is it that these same people (if the creatures of the high priest be not only intended) should, about five days after, change their hosannas for, Away with him! crucify him! crucify him! How fickle is the multitude! Even when they get right, there is but little hope that they will continue so long.
