entries.95b3165db8b357719e80099e3fad492fe1553738: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.21.33" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.21.33" sID="gen101531" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.33">Matthew 21:33</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Hear another parable. </hi>The words of Luke are somewhat different; for he says that Christ <hi type="italic">spoke to the people, </hi>while here the discourse is addressed to the priests and scribes. But the solution is easy; for, though Christ <hi type="italic">spoke against them, </hi>he exposed their baseness in the presence of all the people. Mark says that Christ <hi type="italic">began to speak by parables, </hi>but leaves out what was first in order, as also in other passages he gives only a part of the whole. The substance of this parable is, that it is no new thing, if the priests and the other rulers of the Church wickedly endeavor to defraud God of his right; for long ago they practiced the same kind of robbery towards the prophets, and now they are ready to <hi type="italic">slay his Son; </hi>but they will not go unpunished, for God will arise to defend his right. The object is two-fold; first, to reproach the priests with base and wicked ingratitude; and, secondly, to remove the offense which would be occasioned by his approaching death. For, by means of a false title, they had gained such influence over simple persons and the ignorant multitude, that the religion of the Jews depended on their will and decision. Christ therefore forewarns the weak, and shows that, as so many prophets, one after another, had formerly been slain by the priests, no one ought to be distressed, if a similar instance were exhibited in his own person. But let us now examine it in detail.<div eID="gen101532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101533" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">A man planted a vineyard. </hi>This comparison frequently occurs in Scripture. With respect to the present passage, Christ only means that, while God appoints pastors over his Church, he does <hi type="italic">not </hi>convey his right to others, but acts in the same manner as if a <hi type="italic">proprietor </hi>were to <hi type="italic">let a vineyard </hi>or <hi type="italic">field </hi>to a <hi type="italic">husbandman, </hi>who would labor in the cultivation of it, and make an annual return. As he complains by Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.5.4">5:4</reference>) and Jeremiah, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.2.21">2:21</reference>,) that he had received no fruit from the <hi type="italic">vine </hi>on the cultivation of which he had bestowed so much labor and expense; so in this passage he accuses the vine-dressers themselves, who, like base swindlers, appropriate to themselves the produce of the <hi type="italic">vineyard. </hi>Christ says that the <hi type="italic">vineyard </hi>was well furnished, and in excellent condition, when the <hi type="italic">husbandmen </hi>received it from the hands of the <hi type="italic">proprietor. </hi>By this statement he presents no slight aggravation of their crime; for the more generously he had acted toward them, the more detestable was their ingratitude. Paul employs the same argument, when he wishes to exhort pastors to be diligent in the discharge of their duty, that they are stewards, chosen to govern the house of God, which is the<div eID="gen101533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101534" type="x-p"/>pillar and round of truth, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Tim.3.16">1 Timothy 3:16</reference>.)<div eID="gen101534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101535" type="x-p"/>And properly; for the more honorable and illustrious their condition is, they lie under so much the deeper obligations to God, not to be indolent in their work. So much the more detestable (as we have already said) is the baseness of those who pour contempt on the great kindness of God, and on the great honor which they have already received from Him.<div eID="gen101535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101536" type="x-p"/>God <hi type="italic">planted a vineyard,</hi> <note n="43"> <div sID="gen101537" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Son vigne</foreign>;” — “His vineyard.”<div eID="gen101537" type="x-p"/> </note> when, remembering his gratuitous adoption, he brought the people out of Egypt, separated them anew to be his inheritance, and called them to the hope of eternal salvation, promising to be their God and Father; for this is the <hi type="italic">planting </hi>of which Isaiah speaks, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.60.21 Bible:Isa.61.3">60:21; 61:3</reference>.) By the <hi type="italic">wine-press </hi>and the <hi type="italic">tower </hi>are meant the aids which were added for strengthening the faith of the people in the doctrine of the Law, such as, sacrifices and other ritual observances; for God, like a careful and provident head of a family, has left no means untried for granting to his Church all necessary protection.<div eID="gen101536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101538" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And let it to husbandmen. </hi>God might indeed of himself, without the agency of men, preserve his Church in good order; but he takes men for his ministers, and makes use of their hands. Thus, of old, he appointed priests to be, as it were, cultivators of the <hi type="italic">vineyard. </hi>But the wonder is, that Christ compares the prophets to servants, who are sent, after the vintage, to demand the fruit; <note n="44"> <div sID="gen101539" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Le fruit de la vigne</foreign>;” — “the fruit of the vine.”<div eID="gen101539" type="x-p"/> </note> for we know that they too were <hi type="italic">vine-dressers, </hi>and that they held a charge in common with the priests. I reply, it was not necessary for Christ to be careful or exact in describing the resemblance or contrariety between those two orders. The priests were certainly appointed at first on the condition of thoroughly cultivating the Church by sound doctrine; but as they neglected the work assigned them, either through carelessness or ignorance, the prophets were sent as an extraordinary supply, to clear the vine from weeds, to lop off the superfluous wood, and in other ways to make up for the neglect of the priests; and, at the same time, severely to reprove the people, to raise up decayed piety, to awaken drowsy souls, and to bring back the worship of God and a new life. And what else was this than to demand the revenue which was due to God from his vineyard? All this Christ applies justly and truly to his purpose; for the regular and permanent government of his Church was not in the hands of the prophets, but was always held by the priests; just as if lazy <hi type="italic">husbandman, </hi>while he neglected cultivation, claimed the place to which he had been once appointed, under the plea of possession.<div eID="gen101538" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.21.33" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101531" osisID="Matt.21.33" type="section"/>
entries.71d55b32a72efb0bddb80aa66a143598cd0fbdac: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.21.35" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.21.35" sID="gen101540" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">35.</hi> <hi type="italic">And wounded one, and killed another. </hi>Here Mark andLuke differ a little from Matthew<hi type="italic">;</hi> for while Matthew mentions many servants, all of whom were ill-treated and insulted, and says that <hi type="italic">afterwards other servants were sent more numerous than the first, Mark </hi>and Luke mention but one at a time, as if the <hi type="italic">servants </hi>had been sent, not two or three together, but one after another. But though all the three Evangelists have the same object in view, namely, to show that the Jews will dare to act towards the Son in the same manner as they have repeatedly done towards the prophets, Matthew explains the matter more at large, namely, that God, by sending a multitude of prophets, contended with the malice of the priests. <note n="45"> <div sID="gen101542" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que Dieu ne s’est point lassé pour la cruauté des sacrificateurs, d’envoyer des prophetes; mais les suscitant comme par troupes, a combatu contre leur malice</foreign>;” — “That God did not, on account of the cruelty of the priests, fail to send prophets; but raising them up — as it were — in troops, fought against their malice.”<div eID="gen101542" type="x-p"/> </note> Hence it appears how obstinate their malice was, for the correction of which no remedies were of any avail. <note n="46"> <div sID="gen101543" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Veu que tous les mayens et remedes que Dieu y a employez n’ont rien servi</foreign>;” — “since all the means and remedies which God employed for it were of no avail.”<div eID="gen101543" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen101541" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.21.35" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101540" osisID="Matt.21.35" type="section"/>
entries.5447484e1a36848b0a8da72a0fd17d62d8d24f43: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.21.37" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.21.37" sID="gen101544" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">37.</hi> <hi type="italic">They will reverence my son. </hi>Strictly speaking, indeed, this thought does not apply to God; for He knew what would happen, and was not deceived by the expectation of a more agreeable result; but it is customary, <note n="47"> <div sID="gen101546" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est la coustume de l’Escriture</foreign>;” — “it is the custom of Scripture.”<div eID="gen101546" type="x-p"/> </note> especially in parables, to ascribe to Him human feelings. And yet this was not added without reason; for Christ intended to represent, as in a mirror, how deplorable their impiety was, of which it was too certain a proof, that they rose in diabolical rage against the Son of God, who had come to bring them back to a sound mind. <note n="48"> <div sID="gen101547" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui estoit venu pour les retirer de leurs meschantes façons de faire</foreign>;” — “who had come to withdraw them from their wicked courses of life.”<div eID="gen101547" type="x-p"/> </note> As they had formerly, as far as lay in their power, driven God from his inheritance by the cruel murder of the prophets, so it was the crowning point of all their crimes to <hi type="italic">slay the Son, </hi>that they might reign, as in a house which wanted an heir. Certainly the chief reason why the priests raged against Christ was, that, they might not lose their tyranny, which might be said to be their prey; <note n="49"> <div sID="gen101548" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pource qu’ils avoyent peur de perdre la proye; c’est a dire, de dimineur quelque chose de leur tyrannie</foreign>;” — “because they were afraid of losing the prey; that is to say, of diminishing something of their tyranny.”<div eID="gen101548" type="x-p"/> </note> for he it is by whom God chooses to govern, and to whom He has given all authority.<div eID="gen101545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101549" type="x-p"/>The Evangelists differ also a little in the conclusion. For Matthew relates that he drew from them the confession, by which they condemned themselves; while Mark says simply that Christ declared what punishment must await <hi type="italic">servants </hi>so unprincipled and wicked. Luke differs, at first sight, more openly, by saying that they turned away with horror from the punishment which Christ had threatened. But if we examine the meaning more closely, there is no contradiction; for, in regard to the punishment which such servants deserved, there can be no doubt that they agreed with Christ, but when they perceived that both the crime and the punishment were made to apply to themselves, they deprecated that application.<div eID="gen101549" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.21.37" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101544" osisID="Matt.21.37" type="section"/>
entries.52ba01b2c1628b9e3a21b79b2d481988d6657aa8:
42. Have you never read in the Scriptures? We must remember what we said a little before, that, as the priests and scribes kept the people devoted to them, it was a principle current among them, that they alone were competent to judge and decide as to the future redemption, so that no one ought to be received as Messiah, unless he were approved and sanctioned by their voice. They therefore maintain that what Christ had said is impossible, that they would slay the son and heir of the proprietor of the vineyard. But Christ confirms his statement by the testimony of Scripture, and the interrogation is emphatic, as if he had said, “You reckon it highly absurd to say that it is possible for the vine dressers to conspire wickedly against the Son of God. But what then? Did the Scripture (Psalm 118:22) foretell that he would be received with joy, and favor, and applause; or did it not, on the contrary, foretell that the rulers themselves would oppose him?”
The passage which he quotes is taken from the same psalm from which had been taken that joyful exclamation,
“Ceste priere de louange;” — “that prayer of praise.”
Save,
Our author alludes to the word Hosanna, (ὡσαννὰ) which he had explained (Harmony, vol. 2, p. 452) to be formed, by a slight alteration of the sound, from a Hebrew phrase used in the 118 Psalm, Hoshiana (הושיע נא,) Save now, we beseech thee. — Ed.
O Lord. Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord. That it is a prediction of the reign of the Messiah is evident from this consideration, that David was appointed by God to be king, on the condition that his throne would remain forever, so long as the sun and moon would shine in heaven, and that, when decayed, it would again be restored by the favor of God to its former prosperity. Since, therefore, that psalm contains a description of the reign of David, there is also added the perpetuity of it, on which the restoration depends. If the discourse had related to any temporal reign, Christ would have acted improperly in applying it to himself. But we must also observe what sort of reign God raised up in the person of David. It was that which He would establish in the true Messiah to the end of the world; for that ancient anointing was but a shadow. Hence we infer that what was done in the person of David was a prelude and figure of Christ.
Let us now return to the words of the psalm. The scribes and priests reckoned it incredible that Christ should be rejected
“Ne pouvoient croire que Christ peust estre rejetté;” — “could not believe that Christ could be rejected.”
by the rulers of the Church. But he proves from the psalm, that he would be placed on his throne by the wonderful power of God, contrary to the will of men, and that this had already been shadowed out in David, whom, though rejected by the nobles, God took to give an instance and proof of what he would at length do in his Christ. The prophet takes the metaphor from buildings; for, since the Church is God’s sanctuary, Christ, on whom it is founded, is justly called the corner stone; that is, the stone which supports the whole weight of the building. If one were to examine minutely every thing that relates to Christ, the comparison would not apply in every part; but it is perfectly appropriate, for on him the salvation of the Church rests, and by him its condition is preserved. And therefore the other prophets followed the same form of expression, particularly Isaiah and Daniel. But Isaiah makes the closest allusion to this passage, when he represents God as thus speaking,
Lo, I lay in Zion a foundation-stone, a precious and elect stone, against which both houses of Israel shall stumble! (Isaiah 28:16.)
The same mode of expression frequently occurs in the New Testament.
The amount of it therefore is, that the kingdom of God will be founded on a stone, which the builders themselves will reject as unsuitable and useless; and the meaning is, that the Messiah, who is the foundation of the safety of the Church, will not be chosen by the ordinary suffrages of men, but that, when God shall miraculously raise him up by a secret and unknown power, the rulers, to whom has been committed the care of the building, will oppose and persecute him. There are two things here which we ought to consider. First, that we may not be perplexed by the wicked attempts of men, who rise up to hinder the reign of Christ, God has warned us beforehand that this will happen. Secondly, whatever may be the contrivances of men, God has at the same time declared, that in setting up the kingdom of Christ, His power will be victorious. Both ought to be carefully observed by us. It appears to be monstrous that the Author of salvation should be rejected, not by strangers, but by those who belonged to his own household, — not by the ignorant multitude, but by the rulers themselves, who hold the government of the Church. Against such strange madness of men our faith ought to be fortified, that it may not give way through the novelty of the occurrence. We now perceive how useful that prediction is, which relieves godly minds from the terror that would otherwise be produced by the mournful spectacle. For nothing is more unreasonable than that the members should rise up against the head, the vine-dressers against the proprietor, the counselors against their king, and that the builders should reject the foundation of the building.
That stone is made the head of the corner. Still more emphatic is this clause, in which God declares that the wicked, by rejecting Christ, will avail nothing, but that his rank will remain unimpaired. The design of it is, that believers, relying on that promise, may safely look down with contempt and derision on the wicked pride of men; for when they have made all their contrivances, Christ will still, ill opposition to their wishes, retain the place which the Father has appointed to him. How fiercely soever he may be assailed by those who appear to possess honor and dignity, he will nevertheless remain in his own rank, and will abate nothing on account of their wicked contempt. In short, the authority of God will prevail, that he may be the elect and precious stone, which supports the Church of God, his kingdom and temple. The stone is said to be made the head of the corner, not that he is only a part of the building, (since it is evident from other passages that the Church is entirely founded on Him alone,) but the prophet merely intended to state that he will be the chief support of the building. Some go into ingenious arguments about the word corner, that Christ is placed in the corner, because he unites two separate walls, the Gentiles and Jews. But in my opinion, David meant nothing more than that the corner-stone supports the chief weight of the building.
It may now be asked, How does the Spirit call those men builders, who are so strongly bent on the ruin and destruction of the temple of God? For Paul boasts of having been an honest builder, because he founded the Church on Christ alone, (1 Corinthians 3:10, 11.) The answer is easy. Though they are unfaithful in the execution of the office committed to them, yet he gives them this title with respect to their calling. Thus the name prophet is often given to deceivers, and those who devour the flock like wolves are called pastors. And so far is this from conferring honor on them, that it renders them detestable, when they utterly overthrow the temple of God, which they were appointed to build. Hence we draw a useful warning, that the lawful calling does not prevent those who ought to have been the ministers of Christ from being sometimes his base and wicked enemies. The legal priesthood had certainly been appointed by God, and the Lord had bestowed on the Levites permission to govern the Church. Did they therefore discharge their office faithfully? or ought the godly to have obeyed them by renouncing Christ?
Let the Pope now go with his mitered bishops, and let them boast that they ought to be believed in all things, because they occupy the place of pastors. Even granting that they were lawfully called to the government of the Church, yet they have no right to claim any thing more than to hold the title of prelates of the Church. But even the title of calling does not belong to them; for, in order to raise them to that tyranny, it would be necessary that the whole order of the Church should be overturned. And even though they might justly claim ordinary jurisdiction, yet, if they overturn the sacred house of God, it is only in name that they must be reckoned builders. Nor does it always happen that Christ is rejected by those who are entrusted with the government of the Church; for not only were there many godly priests under the Law, but also, under the reign of Christ, there are some pastors who labor diligently and honestly in building the Church; but as it was necessary that this prediction should be fulfilled, that the builders should reject the stone, wisdom must be exercised in distinguishing between them. And the Holy Spirit has expressly warned us, that none may be mistaken as to an empty title or the dignity of calling.
This has been done by the Lord, As it is a matter too far removed from the ordinary judgment of men, that the pastors of the Church should themselves reject the Son of God from being their Prince, the prophet refers it to the secret purpose of God, which, though we cannot comprehend it by our senses, we ought to contemplate and admire. Let us therefore understand, that this cuts short every question, and that every man is expressly forbidden to judge and measure the nature of Christ’s kingdom by the reason of the flesh; for what folly is it to wish to subject to the capacity of our mind a miracle which the prophet exhorts us to adore? Will you then receive nothing but what appears to yourself to be probable, in reference to the kingdom of Christ, the commencement of which the Holy Spirit declares to be a mystery worthy of the highest admiration, because it is concealed from the eyes of men? So then, whenever the question relates to the origin, restoration, condition, and the whole safety of the Church, we must not consult our senses,
“Qu’il nous souviene de ne nous arrester point a ce que nos sens pervent comprende;” — “let us remember not to stop at what our senses can comprehend.”
but must honor the power of God by admiring his hidden work.
“Son œuvre incomprehensible;” — “his incomprehensible work.”
There is also an implied contrast between God and men; for not only are we commanded to embrace the wonderful method of governing the Church, because it is the work of God, but we are likewise withdrawn from a foolish reverence for men, which frequently obscures the glow of God; as if the prophet had said, that however magnificent may be the titles which men bear, it is wicked in any man to oppose them to God.
This furnishes a refutation of the diabolical wickedness of the Papists, who do not scruple to prefer to the word of God a decision of their pretended Church. For on what does the authority of the word of God depend, according to them, but on the opinion of men, so that no more power is left to God than what the Church is pleased to allow him? Far otherwise does the Spirit instruct us by this passage namely, that as soon as the majesty of God
“La majesté du Fils de Dieu;” — “the majesty of the Son of God.”
appears, the whole world ought to be silent.
entries.f174cf0e5490f0e6b4f4ff15fb1cbb0edb85fd56: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.21.43" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.21.43" sID="gen101568" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101569" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">43.</hi> <hi type="italic">Therefore I say to you. </hi>Hitherto Christ directed his discourse to rulers and governors, but in presence of the people. Now, however, he addresses in the same manner the people themselves, and not without reason, for they had been the companions and assistants of the priests and scribes in hindering the grace of God. It was from the priests, no doubt, that the evil arose, but the people had already deserved, on account of their sins, to have such corrupt and degenerate pastors. Besides, the whole body was infected, as it were, by a similar malice to resist God. This is the reason why Christ denounces against all indiscriminately the dreadful vengeance of God; for as the priests were inflated with the desire of holding the highest power, so the rest of the people gloried on the ground of having been adopted. Christ now declares that God was not bound to them, and, therefore, that he will convey to another the honor of which they rendered themselves unworthy. And this, no doubt, was once spoken to them, but was written for the sake of all of us, that, if God choose us to be His people, we may not grow wanton through a vain and wicked confidence in the flesh, but may endeavor, on our part, to perform the duties which he enjoins on his children;<div eID="gen101569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101570" type="x-p"/>for if he spared not the natural branches, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.11.21">Romans 11:21</reference>,)<div eID="gen101570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101571" type="x-p"/>what will he do with those which were engrafted? The Jews thought that the kingdom of God dwelt among them by hereditary right, and therefore they adhered obstinately to their vices. We have unexpectedly come into their room contrary to nature, and therefore much less is the kingdom of God bound to us, if it be not rooted in true godliness.<div eID="gen101571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101572" type="x-p"/>Now as our minds ought to be struck with terror by the threatening of Christ, that those who have profaned the kingdom of God will be deprived of it, so the perpetuity of that kingdom, which is here described, may afford comfort to all the godly. For by these words Christ assures us that, though the ungodly destroyed the worship of God among themselves, they would never cause the name of Christ to be abolished, or true religion to perish; for God, in whose hand are all the ends of the earth, will find elsewhere a dwelling and habitation for his kingdom. We ought also to learn from this passage, that the Gospel is not preached in order that it may lie barren and inoperative, but that it may yield fruit.<div eID="gen101572" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.21.43" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101568" osisID="Matt.21.43" type="section"/>
entries.4cdc4901f56d2faca832167682d6d8e7f16b5a77: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.21.44" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.21.44" sID="gen101573" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101574" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">44.</hi> <hi type="italic">And he who shall fall on this stone. </hi>Christ confirms more fully the former statement, that he suffers no loss or diminution when he is rejected by the wicked, because, though their obstinacy were like a stone or like iron, yet by his own hardness he will break them, and therefore he will be the more highly glorified in their destruction. He perceived in the Jews an astonishing obstinacy, and therefore it was necessary that this kind of punishment should be described to them in an alarming manner, that they might not flatter themselves, while they thus dashed against him. This doctrine partly instructs us to give ourselves up gently, with a mild and tractable heart, to the dominion of Christ, and partly fortifies us against the obstinacy and furious attacks of the wicked, for whom there awaits a dreadful end.<div eID="gen101574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101575" type="x-p"/>Those persons are said to <hi type="italic">fall upon </hi>Christ, who rush forward to destroy him; not that they occupy a more elevated position than he does, but because their madness carries them so far, that they endeavor to attack Christ as if he were below them. But Christ tells them that all that they will gain by it is, that by the very conflict they will be <hi type="italic">broken. </hi>But when they have thus proudly exalted themselves, he tells them that another thing will happen, which is, that they will be <hi type="italic">bruised </hi>under the <hi type="italic">stone, </hi>against which they so insolently dashed themselves.<div eID="gen101575" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.21.44" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101573" osisID="Matt.21.44" type="section"/>

45. They knew that he spoke of them. The Evangelists show how little success Christ had, that we may not wonder if the doctrine of the Gospel does not bring all men, in the present day, to yield obedience to God. Let us also learn that it is impossible but that the rage of ungodly men will be more and more inflamed by threatenings; for as God seals his word on our hearts, so also it is a hot iron to wound bad consciences, in consequence of which their ungodliness is the more inflamed. We ought therefore to pray that he would subdue us to voluntary fear, lest the mere knowledge of his vengeance should exasperate us the more. When they are restrained solely by the dread of the people from laying their hands on Christ, let us learn that God had laid a bridle on them; from which also arises a very delightful consolation to believers, when they learn that God protects them, and constantly enables them to escape from the jaws of death.
MATTHEW 22:15-22; MARK 12:13-17; LUKE 20:20-26
Matthew 22:15-22
Mark 12:13-17
Luke 20:20-26
15. Then the Pharisees went away, and took counsel how they might entrap him in his words. 16. And they send to him their disciples, with the Herodians, saying, Master, we know that thou art true, and teachest the way of God in truth, and carest not for any man; for thou regardest not the person of men. 17. Tell us then, What thinkest thou? Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not? 18. But Jesus, perceiving their wickedness, saith, Why do you tempt me, hypocrites? 19. Show me the tribute money. And they presented to him a denarius. 20. And he saith to them, Whose is this image and inscription? 21. They say to him, Caesar’s. Then said he to them, Render therefore to Caesar the things which are Caesar’s, and to God the things which are God’s. 22. And having heard these things, they wondered, and left him, and went away.
13. And they send to him certain Pharisees and Herodians, to entrap him in his words 14. And they, when they came, said to him, Master, we know that thou art true, and carest not for any man; for thou regardest not the person of men, but teachest the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not? Shall we give, or shall we not give? 15. But he, knowing their hypocrisy, said to them, Why do you tempt me? Bring me a denarius, that I may see it. 16. And they brought it; and he saith to them, Whose is this image and inscription? And they said to him, Caesars. 17. And Jesus answering said to them, Render to Caesar those things which are Caesar’s, and to God those things which are God’s.
“Et n’es point accepteur de personnes;” — “and art not an accepter of persons.”
And they wondered at him.
“Rendez à Caesar ce qui est à Caesar, et à Dieu ce qui est à Dieu;” — “render to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”
20. And they watched him, and sent spies, who would pretend to be righteous men, to entrap him in his words, and to deliver him to the authority and power of the governor. 21. And they put a question to him, saying, Master, we know that thou sayest and teachest uprightly, and regardest not a person,
“Et furent esmerveillez de luy;” — “and they were astonished at him.”
but teachest the way of God in truth. 22. Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not? 23. And having perceived their craftiness, he said to them, Why do you tempt me? 24. Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription hath it? They answering said, Caesar’s. 25. And he said to them, Render therefore to Caesar those things which are Caesar’s, and to God those things which are God’s. 26. And they could not find fault with his words in presence of the people; and wondering at his reply, they were silent.

entries.2cb8d7ce74bfebecf3129a48e987c6b9144b3de0:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="21" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. XXI.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 ANd when they drew nigh unto Jerusalem, and were come up to Bethphage, unto the mount of Olives, then sent Jesus two disciples.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 Saying unto them, Go into the village over against you, and straightway, ye shall find an ass tyed, and a colt with her; loose <ns0:hi>them,</ns0:hi> and bring <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> unto me.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 And if any man say ought unto you, ye shall say, The Lord hath need of them, and straightway he will send them.<ns0:note place="bottom">This Famous story of our Lords entrance into <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> is recorded by <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> also, by <ns0:hi>Mark, Ch.</ns0:hi> 11.1. By <ns0:hi>Luke, Ch.</ns0:hi> 19.29. There is little difference in their Rela<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of it thus far, afterwards we shall find more: I shall consider what they all say, that I may at once give the story perfect. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Bethpage</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> He saith, <ns0:hi>You shall find a Colt tyed, whereon never Man sate. Luke</ns0:hi> hardly varieth at all from <ns0:hi>Mark,</ns0:hi> at least in nothing considerable. Our Lord was come now very nigh <ns0:hi>Ierusalem, Bethany</ns0:hi> was but fifteen Furlongs from <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> that was about two miles wanting an eighth part. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 11.18<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> it was the Town of <ns0:hi>Lazarus, Ioh.</ns0:hi> 11.1. <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> names only <ns0:hi>Bethpage,</ns0:hi> which was a place at the same distance, at the Foot of the <ns0:hi>Mount of Olives,</ns0:hi> so called from the plenty of <ns0:hi>Olive-Trees</ns0:hi> growing there; this <ns0:hi>Mount</ns0:hi> was betwixt <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Bethpage:</ns0:hi> It is like our Saviour was at both these Towns, for <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> nameth both, from one of them he sendeth two of his Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciples, to a Village near hand; telling them, they should there find, at their Entrance in, <ns0:hi>an Ass tyed with a Colt, on which yet never Man sate. Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> only mention the Colt, because Christ rode only upon the Colt. <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> mentions the Ass, for the fulfilling of the Prophecy, of which we shall hear in the next Verses. <ns0:hi>Loose them, and bring them to me: And if any Man say ought to you</ns0:hi> (which he knew they would, and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> tell us they did) <ns0:hi>You shall say, the Lord hath need of him.</ns0:hi> Not our Lord, but <ns0:hi>the Lord</ns0:hi> of Heaven and Earth; whose are the Cattel upon a thousand Hills, <ns0:hi>hath need of him,</ns0:hi> not for any Wea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riness; he who had Travelled on foot from <ns0:hi>Galilee</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> could have gone the other two miles: But that he might enter into <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> as was Prophecied of him, <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 9.9. <ns0:hi>And he will straightway send him.</ns0:hi> The words are so, as may be understood as a Promise of Christ to send him back, but it is more likely they are intended, as an assurance to the Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciples, that the owners would make no Difficulty to send them. These Instructions (considered with the Success) were an evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dent Argument of Christ's <ns0:hi>Divine Nature.</ns0:hi> Who could tell all particular Circumstances, and also which way the Heart of man would incline.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:256" />4 All this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Tell ye the daughter of Zion, Behold, thy King cometh unto thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass, and a colt, the foal of an ass.<ns0:note place="bottom">The Words are, <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 9.9. <ns0:hi>Rejoyce greatly O Daughter of Zion, shout O Daughter of Ierusalem, Behold, thy King cometh unto thee: He is just, and having Salvation, Lowly, and riding upon an Ass, and upon a Colt the Foal of an Ass.</ns0:hi> The Evangelist quoteth no more of them, then ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved for his purpose. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> in the short Account, he giveth of this our Saviour's entrance, quoteth them shorter. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 12.15. The former part of the Words are found, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 62.11. The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> agree this <ns0:hi>Prophecy</ns0:hi> to respect the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> tho they were so blinded, as not to see it was fulfilled in Christ. <ns0:hi>Tell you the Daughter of Zion,</ns0:hi> Prophecy you to the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> to the Citizens, and Inhabitants of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> Behold, <ns0:hi>Thy King cometh to thee.</ns0:hi> Thy spiritual King, having Salvation, the King promised, and foretold, that shall bring Salvation, <ns0:hi>cometh,</ns0:hi> that is, shall shortly come to thee for thy Profit and Advan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tage. And you shall know him by this. He shall come <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>Poor, Afflicted, Meek, Lowly,</ns0:hi> sitting upon an <ns0:hi>Ass,</ns0:hi> an Ass used to bear Burdens (so the Word signifies) and a <ns0:hi>Colt the Foal of an Ass:</ns0:hi> Not upon both, they are <ns0:hi>Exegetical</ns0:hi> of each other. The first denoted the <ns0:hi>Species of</ns0:hi> the Beast, the second its Age: There was not any Prophecy of <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> more plainly fulfilled than this. <ns0:hi>Asses</ns0:hi> were of Old Beasts, that Great Persons used to ride on, <ns0:hi>Iud.</ns0:hi> 10.4. <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 12.14. But after <ns0:hi>Solomons</ns0:hi> time, the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> got a Breed of Horses; so as only Poor people rode upon Asses, mostly reserved for Burdens; whom could the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> possibly expect to see coming, riding into <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> under the Notion of a <ns0:hi>King</ns0:hi> bringing them Salvation, in so little State, <ns0:hi>upon the Foal of an Ass,</ns0:hi> but the Person Prophe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cied of by <ns0:hi>Zachariah, Ch.</ns0:hi> 9.9. whom they themselves Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fess to be the <ns0:hi>Messiah?</ns0:hi> And had not there been a strange Veil upon their Hearts, <ns0:hi>Herods</ns0:hi> Courtiers, and <ns0:hi>Pilates</ns0:hi> might have understood, his Kingdom was not of this World, nor he such a King, as threatned their <ns0:hi>Grandeur.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mar. 11.2.</ns0:note> And the disciples went, and did as Jesus commanded them.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 11.4. <ns0:hi>And they went their way, and found the Colt tyed by the Door without, in a place where two ways met, and they loose him. And certain of them that stood there, said unto them, What do you loosing the Colt? And they said unto them, even as Iesus had Commanded; and they let them go. Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 19.1.32. <ns0:hi>And they that were sent went away, and found even as he had said unto them; and as they were loosing the Colt, the Owners thereof said unto them, Why loose you the Colt? And they said, The Lord hath need of him.</ns0:hi> The true Obedience of Christ's Disciples, is to be learned from the Pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctice of these two Disciples: They dispute not the Commands of their Lord, nor make Objections, nor raise any Disputes, nor are afraid of any Danger to themselves, they went, and that speedily, and are exact to what their Lord had Command<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed them, accordingly they find, as he had said, they loose the Colt, the owner seeing them, asks why they loose the Colt. <ns0:hi>They tell him the Lord had need of him.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 And brought the ass, and the colt, and put on them their cloths, and set <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> thereon.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 And a very great multitude spread their garments in the way, others cut down branches from the trees, and strewed <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> in the way.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And the multitudes that went before, and that followed, cryed, saying, Hosanna to the son of David, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 23.39.</ns0:note> Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord, Hosanna in the highest.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 11.7. <ns0:hi>And they brought the Colt to Ie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sus, and cast their Garments on him, and he sate upon him. And many spread their Garments in the way, and others cut down Branches of the Trees and strewed them in the way: And they that went before, and they that followed, Cryed, Saying, Hosanna! Blessed is he that com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth in the Name of the Lord. Blessed be the Kingdom of our Father David, that cometh in the Name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest. Luke</ns0:hi> hath it yet with more Cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumstances, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 19.35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40. <ns0:hi>And they brought him to Iesus, and they cast their Garments upon the Colt, and they set Iesus thereon: And as he went, they spread their Cloaths in the way: And when he was nigh, even now at the Descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole mul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />titude, of the Disciples, began to Rejoyce, and Praise God with a loud Voice, for all the mighty Works they had seen, saying, Blessed be the King, that cometh in the Name of the Lord, Peace in Heaven, and Glory in the Highest. And some of the Pharisees from amongst the multitudes, said unto him. Master rebuke thy Disciples. And he answered and said unto them, If these should hold their Peace, the stones would immediately Cry out. Iohn</ns0:hi> also gives us some Ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count of this, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 12.12, 13. <ns0:hi>On the next day much Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple that were come to the Feast, when they had heard that Iesus was coming to Ierusalem, took Branches of Palm Trees, and went forth to meet him, and Cryed, Hosanna: Blessed be the King of Israel, that cometh in the Name of the Lord.</ns0:hi> They bring <ns0:hi>the Ass, and the Colt to Iesus,</ns0:hi> who had no Saddle, no costly Furniture for him; they were glad to lay on the Asses back some of their Garments, and to set Christ upon the Colt. And in a kind of a natural Country Triumph, made up without any kind of Art, some threw their Cloths in his way, some cut down Boughs of Trees (<ns0:hi>Palm Trees</ns0:hi> saith <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi>) with these they bestrew the way. Christ at <ns0:hi>Bethany</ns0:hi> in his Journey, had done a Famous Miracle, raising up <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> from the Dead. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 12.18. the Fame of this, made many that were in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> who were come thither against the Passover time (for <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 12.1. it was but <ns0:hi>six Days before the Passover</ns0:hi>) go out to meet him, and joyned with those, who came along with him from <ns0:hi>Betha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny,</ns0:hi> they Cryed all along as they came, <ns0:hi>Hosanna to the Son of David. Blessed is he that cometh in the Name of the Lord. Hosanna in the Highest. Blessed is the King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom of our Father David. Peace in Heaven, and Glory in the Highest.</ns0:hi> Many of these Expressions, seem to be taken out of <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 118.24, 25, 26. Their laying the Garments up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on the Ass, and throwing them in the way, was a Custom they used towards Princes, as appears, not only by many Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cords out of profane Authors, but from 2 <ns0:hi>Kin.</ns0:hi> 9.13. where the like was done to <ns0:hi>Iehu,</ns0:hi> upon his being anointed <ns0:hi>King</ns0:hi> over <ns0:hi>Israel.</ns0:hi> For the Acclamations, they were also such as were usual to Princes: Whether <ns0:hi>Hosanna</ns0:hi> signifieth, <ns0:hi>Save now</ns0:hi>: Or, <ns0:hi>Help! We pray:</ns0:hi> Or, whether it was a <ns0:hi>Term</ns0:hi> by which they expressed their Desire of good Success, or Prospe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity to the Person, to whom they apply'd it: Or, whether it was the Name of some Song used in their Festivals, or it sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifies, <ns0:hi>Boughs, &c.</ns0:hi> is not much Material; they by this <ns0:hi>Ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clamation,</ns0:hi> acknowledged him a King, the Son of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>; they Blessed him, they wished him Peace, Honour and Glory. This was the <ns0:hi>Acclamation</ns0:hi> of the multitude, who doubtless had but a small, and imperfect knowledge of the Divine Nature of Christ, but yet looked on him, as the <ns0:hi>Son of David,</ns0:hi> as the <ns0:hi>Messiah.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> (some of which it seemeth had mixed themselves with this multitude, were troubled at the <ns0:hi>Acclamation,</ns0:hi> and (as <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> tells us) speak to Christ to rebuke them; but he answereth, <ns0:hi>If these should hold their Peace, the stones would immediately Cry out.</ns0:hi> It is a <ns0:hi>Prover<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bial</ns0:hi> Expression, the Sense of which is alone to be attend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed. The Sense is this: The time is come, set by my Father for the Publication of my Kingdom, and declaring what I am, and when Gods time is come, the thing must come to pass, by one mean or another: If these Children of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> should hold their Peace, God is able of these stones to raise up Children to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> and they should do the same thing, publish me as the Son of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>King</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Zion.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 And when he was come into Jerusalem,<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mar. 11.15. Luk. 19.45. John 2.13.15<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 18.</ns0:note> all the city was moved, saying, Who is this?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 And the multitude said, This is Jesus, the prophet, of Nazareth of Galilee.<ns0:note place="bottom">Such an unusual sight might well affect a great number in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> with Admiration and Astonishment; the People especially, giving Honour to him as a <ns0:hi>King,</ns0:hi> and calling him the <ns0:hi>Son of David</ns0:hi>; and certainly, but that the Meanness of his Appearance, and Meanness of his Followers, put uninte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ressed Men out of Fear; and gave <ns0:hi>Herod,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> some se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />curity, that there was no Attempt on Foot, against the Ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vil Government: Our Saviour and his Followers would have been apprehended, as Raisers of a <ns0:hi>Sedition</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Rebellion.</ns0:hi> But the multitude now gave him no other Title, than that of Jesus the Prophet; which yet was enough to distinguish him from other Prophets, for he was <ns0:hi>Iesus</ns0:hi> a Saviour, and <ns0:hi>the Prophet</ns0:hi> foretold, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 18.15.18, 19.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold, and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the money changers, and the seats of them that sold doves.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And said, it is written, My house shall be called an house of prayer, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 7.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> but ye have made it a den of theeves.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And the blind, and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.<ns0:note place="bottom">This piece of the History, is related by two of the other Evangelists, but with great difference. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> before this<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> mentioneth a Discourse upon the way, upon our Saviour's first sight of the City, and his Prophecy of the Destruction of it; but no other Evangelist mentioning it, I shall pass it over, till I come to his History. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> hath this part of the History thus. <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 11.11. <ns0:hi>And Iesus entred into Ierusalem, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> the Temple,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>when he had looked round about upon all things, and the Even-tide was come, he went out to</ns0:hi> Bethany <ns0:hi>with the twelve. And on the morrow, when they were come from</ns0:hi> Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thany, <ns0:hi>he was hungry,</ns0:hi>—(Then he relates, our Saviours cursing the barren Fig-Tree, which I leave till I come to it in Order, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 15. <ns0:hi>And they come to Ierusalem, and Iesus went into the Temple, and began to cast out them that sold and bought in the Temple; and overthrew the Tables of the Money-Chan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gers, and the Seats of them that sold Doves: And would not suffer that any Man should carry a Vessel through the Temple. And he taught, saying unto them, Is it not written, my House shall be called of all Nations the House of Prayer, but you have made it a Den of Thieves: And when the Even was come he went out of the City, v.</ns0:hi> 19. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 19.45. <ns0:hi>And he went into the Temple, and began to cast out those that sold therein, and those that bought, saying to them, It is writ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten, My House is the House of Prayer, but you have made it a Den of Thieves.—And he taught daily in the Temple.</ns0:hi> It is pla<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>n by all the Evangelists<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> that our Saviour coming to <ns0:hi>Ierusa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lem,</ns0:hi> five days before the Passover, went every night to <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> about two miles off<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and returned in the Morning to the Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, where <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith that <ns0:hi>he taught daily.</ns0:hi> The first day, it should seem by <ns0:hi>Mark,</ns0:hi> that he only came into the <ns0:hi>Temple,</ns0:hi> lookt round about upon all things, and with the twelve went out to lodge at <ns0:hi>Bethany.</ns0:hi> By his going into the <ns0:hi>Temple,</ns0:hi> we must un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand only the <ns0:hi>outward Court,</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:hi>Priests</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Levits</ns0:hi> only might enter into the <ns0:hi>Inner-Court,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Holy Place</ns0:hi>; and the <ns0:hi>High Priest,</ns0:hi> only might enter into the <ns0:hi>Holiest of all.</ns0:hi> Tho <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> mentions not his driving out the Buyers and Sellers the first day, but reciteth it as if it had been done the second day of his coming, yet the best <ns0:hi>Interpreters</ns0:hi> think that it was done the first day, as <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> seem to hint; nor is any thing more usual, than for the Evangelists to set down things out of the Order of time, in which they were done. Some learned Authors in the Hebrew Learning tell us, That in the <ns0:hi>outward Court,</ns0:hi> was a daily Market of such things as the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> used for Sacrifices, <ns0:hi>Wine, Salt, Oyl, Oxen,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sheep:</ns0:hi> But it being but three or four days before the Passover, the Market was much greater, because of the great multitude of Lambs, then to be used. By the Law, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 30.12.15. every one also was to bring an <ns0:hi>half Shekel.</ns0:hi> For this purpose there were <ns0:hi>Tables of Money Changers</ns0:hi>; Men that were furnished with <ns0:hi>half Shekels</ns0:hi> to change with the People, that every one might have his <ns0:hi>half Shekel,</ns0:hi> and those that so changed, allowed some little Profit to those that changed their Money, which gain was called, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>; thence the Changers were called <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, Mony Changers. Those that sold <ns0:hi>Doves</ns0:hi> were there, to furnish the Women that came up to their <ns0:hi>Purifi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cation</ns0:hi> with their <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> according to the Law, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 12.6. This was the reaso<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> that great Market, which our Lord found in the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of the Temple, and it is not likely that our Lord shou<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> these abuses the first day, and take no notice of them, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> the next day and correct them, which makes Interpreter <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> in this Relation post-poned this part of the Histo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> arise two Questions. 1. <ns0:hi>Whether it was unlawful fo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> to sell these things in that part of the Temple.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                           <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, By what Authority did our Saviour do this?</ns0:hi> To <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> it must be said, That had it not been un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lawful, our <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> would not have reproved them, for turning his Fathers <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> and the <ns0:hi>House of Prayer,</ns0:hi> into a place of Mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chandise. Nor would he have driven them out in such a Zeal, overturning the Tables, &c. which he had done also once be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 2.15. The <ns0:hi>Temple</ns0:hi> was built by Gods direction, not only dedicated by Men, but Gods Acceptation of it was testified: It appeareth by <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 2.19. it was a <ns0:hi>Type of Christs Body.</ns0:hi> We know there were <ns0:hi>special Promises</ns0:hi> made to those that did pray to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward it, 1 <ns0:hi>Kin.</ns0:hi> 9.3. God saith, he <ns0:hi>had hallowed it,</ns0:hi> that is, separated it from common use to his Service amongst other things for an <ns0:hi>house of Prayer, Isa.</ns0:hi> 56.7. Now tho we read of no o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther things sold there, but what were useful for Sacrifices, yet this was a Civil use, and a Profanation of that <ns0:hi>Holy Place,</ns0:hi> because there were Market-places in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> in which these things might have been done. It had been against Decency, if the <ns0:hi>Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple</ns0:hi> had not been hallowed in this manner, if such things had been done in the <ns0:hi>Synagogues,</ns0:hi> being places set apart, and commonly used for Gods Worship; but to use the <ns0:hi>Temple</ns0:hi> in this manner, so specially hallowed, was doubtless a great <ns0:hi>Profanation</ns0:hi> of that <ns0:hi>Holy Place.</ns0:hi> As to the second Question: <ns0:hi>By what Authority our Lord, being no publick Magistrate, did these thing<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:hi> I am not so posed to determine that, he being the Eternal Son <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> God, and now in the Exercise of his Regal Power, as I am to give an Ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count how it came to pass, that the <ns0:hi>Priests,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Scribes,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />risees</ns0:hi> never questioned him for what he did; for if any will say, That we presently shall read of their taking Council against him: I reply, But we read of nothing relating to this laid to his Charge. Nor do we read of their Questioning him, when he did the same things before, an Account of which we have in, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 2. For tho I know some say, that our Saviour did this <ns0:hi>Iure Zelotarum.</ns0:hi> That the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> had a Law, That any might punish even to Death, such as profaned the Worship, or Holy things of God; which they justifie from <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 13.9. and the Examples of <ns0:hi>Phine<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />has</ns0:hi> killing <ns0:hi>Z<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>mri</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Kosbi, Numb.</ns0:hi> 25.6. and <ns0:hi>Mattaniah</ns0:hi>'s killing the <ns0:hi>Iew,</ns0:hi> Sacrificing to Idols at <ns0:hi>Modin,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Kings Commissioner,</ns0:hi> of which we read in 2 <ns0:hi>Maccab.</ns0:hi> 2.24, 25. yet this doth no way give me any Satisfaction; for as on the one side, I should not have known how to have defended the Act of <ns0:hi>Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nehas,</ns0:hi> if God had not by and by justified him, nor do I think that the Law in <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 13.9. is to be expounded of private Persons<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> So on the other side, if the <ns0:hi>Priests</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Scribes,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> had not known of some Law that justified our Saviour in this Act, I can hardly conceive they would have so quietly put it up, especially considering that probably their Pront was concerned, if they had for Gain Licensed those Traders, to a place within the Compass of the Temple; as is very probable. Being there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore fully satisfied, that our <ns0:hi>Saviour</ns0:hi> who was <ns0:hi>Lord</ns0:hi> of the Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, and to whom the Spirit was given without measure, did no more, than he might Lawfully do, I am willingly Ignorant how it came to pass, that he met with no opposition in it, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause God hath not pleased in his Word to inform us. It is cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain that he did the thing, and that it was a thing fit to be done, and that he, as the Son of God, had Authority to do it; what made them take it so quietly, I cannot tell, nor is it necessary for us to know, nor of any great advantage.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:257" />15 And when the chief priests, and the scribes, saw the wonderful things that he did, and the chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren crying in the temple, and saying, Hosanna to the Son of David, they were sore displeased.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 And said unto him, Hearest thou what these say? And Jesus saith unto them, Yea, Have ye never read Out of the mouths of babes and suck<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lings, thou hast perfected praise?<ns0:note place="bottom">The other Evangelists say nothing of this part of this Histo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry: The wonderful things here mentioned, are his healing <ns0:hi>the Blind</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Lame,</ns0:hi> of which we read <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14. The Cry of the Children doubtless more displeased them; it was of the same Nature with that of the multitude in the way, and in the Streets when our Lord came into <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> they owned Christ as the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> and gave him Praise, and wished all manner of Felicity to him. The <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> shewing a displeasure at the Acclama<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, Christ referreth them to what was written, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 8.2. there it is thou hast <ns0:hi>Founded,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Ordained strength,</ns0:hi> that is, a solid, and firm Praise: A prediction that from the Testimony of such weak Persons, the Glorious power of Christ should be pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />claimed, and from such mean and despicable beginnings; great and Glorious things should come to pass.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And he left them, and went out of the city into Bethany, and he lodged there.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 Now in the morning, as he returned into the city, he hungred.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And when he saw <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> a fig-tree in the way, he came to it, and found nothing thereon but leaves only, and said unto it, Let no fruit grow on thee, hence forward for ever. And presently the fig-tree withered away.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 And when the disciples saw <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> they marvelled, saying, How soon is the fig-tree withered away?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Jesus answered, and said unto them, Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 paragraph">
                        <ns0:desc>〈1 paragraph〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> and doubt not, ye shall not only do this, <ns0:hi>which is done</ns0:hi> to the fig-tree, but also, if ye shall say to this mountain, Be thou re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />moved, and be thou cast into the sea, it shall be done.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. Mark 11.2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Luke 11.9 1 Joh. 3.22. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 5.14.</ns0:note> all things whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> hath nothing of this passage, but <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> relateth it, with some <ns0:hi>Variation,</ns0:hi> and Additions: The <ns0:hi>Variation</ns0:hi> is only as to time, (as to which the Evangelists were not Curious) <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> relates this Miracle, as done in the Morning of the second day, as Christ and his Disciples returned from <ns0:hi>Bethany</ns0:hi>; so doth <ns0:hi>Mark, Ch.</ns0:hi> 11, 12. but <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> speaks, as if the Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciples discerned it presently Withered. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> mentions it, as not discerned to be Withered, till the next Morning, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 13. <ns0:hi>For the time of Figs was not yet,</ns0:hi> which breeds a Difficulty, why our Saviour should Curse the Fig-tree, for having no Fruit, when the time for its Fruit was not come (of which more by and by.) <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21, 22. That <ns0:hi>Peter calling to remembrance</ns0:hi> his Masters Cursing the Fig-tree, <ns0:hi>saith unto him Master, Behold the Fig-tree which thou Cursedst is Withered away: And Iesus an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swering said unto them. Have faith in God</ns0:hi>: Then repeats the substance of what <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> hath in <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21, 22. to which <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> addeth, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 25, 26. <ns0:hi>And when you stand Praying, forgive, if you have ought against any; that your Father also which is in Heaven, may forgive you your Trespasses. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father which is in Heaven, forgive you your Trespasses.</ns0:hi> When our Lord had been in the Temple, and driven out the Buyers, and Sellers there, he went out of the City to lye at <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> either to avoid the noises of the City (now very full of People, the Passover be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing so nigh) or to get a more private place for Prayer. He returns the next Morning, and being an Hungry, and seeing a Fig-tree in his way, he goes to it, finds it full of Leaves, but no Fruit on it. He saith unto it, <ns0:hi>Never Fruit grow on thee more. Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>For the time of Figs was no<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> yet: Why then doth our Saviour Curse this Tree?</ns0:hi> Some think, that by <ns0:hi>time</ns0:hi> is here meant <ns0:hi>Season</ns0:hi> (as indeed the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> word often signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fieth) these would have the meaning to be<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>For it was not <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Seasonab<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e year for Figs.</ns0:hi> But this rather Augmenteth, than abates the Difficulty; for why should our Saviour Curse it, for having no Figs<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> when the Year was such, as was not Sea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sonable? Others therefore think, that <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> should be <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, then the <ns0:hi>English</ns0:hi> would be, <ns0:hi>Where he was, was a time of Figs.</ns0:hi> For this it is said, 1. That the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> Spirits and Accents were ordinarily left out in ancient Copies, which if they be taken a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />way, the Words are the same. 2. That this was according to Truth, for it was a time of <ns0:hi>Green Figs,</ns0:hi> at least it being near <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and but three or four days before the Passover, about which time they reaped their Corn, as appears from <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 23.16. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 16.9. and it is plain from, <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 2.13. that in the beginning of their Spring, their <ns0:hi>Fig-trees put forth Green Figs.</ns0:hi> But when I consider, that none of the ancient Translations are according to this <ns0:hi>Criticism,</ns0:hi> but as our Translations, I conclude, that the Antients understood it, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> not <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, and it seemeth too bold to interpret the Words contrary to their Unanimous Sense: Others therefore tell us, that Fig-trees, or at least some kind of them (like <ns0:hi>Orange-trees</ns0:hi>) had Leaves and Fruit upon them always, some Green, some half Ripe, some full Ripe, and that these kept on their Leaves all the Winter: So that our Saviour seeing Leaves, might be led to it with an Expe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctation of some Fruit put forth the former Year, for the time for the Ripening of Fruit, of that kind that Year, was not come, and finding none, he Cursed it. Thereby in a Type, shewing what should be done to Barren Souls, who have only Leaves, no true Fruit of Righteousness. Or, what if we should say, that he did not Curse it, with any respect to its want of Fruit, but only to shew his <ns0:hi>Divine Power,</ns0:hi> working a Miracle? <ns0:hi>And presently the Fig-tree Withered away:</ns0:hi> A<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>soon as our Saviour had Cursed it, it began to Wither. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> tells us this was the <ns0:hi>next Morning, Ch.</ns0:hi> 11.20. which made <ns0:hi>Pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter</ns0:hi> say, <ns0:hi>Master behold the Fig-tree which thou Cursedst is Withered away. Matthew</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>When the Disciples saw it, they marvelled saying, How soon is the Fig-tree Wither<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed away?</ns0:hi> Upon this our Saviour telleth <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> and the rest, that if they had Faith, and doubted not, they should not only do that which he had done to the Fig-tree, but <ns0:hi>if they said to that Mountain, be removed and cast into the Sea, it should be done.</ns0:hi> This is interpreted by <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. <ns0:hi>All things whatsoever ye shall ask in Prayer, ye shall receive:</ns0:hi> We met with the like Expression before, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 17.20. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> hath the same, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 11.23. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> hath it, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 17.6. It is an Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pression which ought not to be strained further than to sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifie, That there is nothing conducive to the Glory of God, and our own good, but Believers may receive at the Hand of God, if they can believe without doubting, that what they would have shall come to pass. I see no reason to Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />course of a <ns0:hi>Faith of Miracles,</ns0:hi> as different from other Faith; which only thus differed, that the Disciples (the Apostles I mean) had a Power given them, and a Promise made to them, that they should be able to work miraculous Operations, which is not given to other Christians serving only the particular occa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sions of that time, to give Credit to the Gospel. The Gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral proposition is true, and shall be made Good, to every Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liever: <ns0:hi>That whatsoever Good is made the matter of a Promise</ns0:hi> (such are all Good things) <ns0:hi>shall be given to belie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving Souls, Praying for them.</ns0:hi> But there were of old <ns0:hi>special Promises,</ns0:hi> not made to the People of God in general, but to particular Persons, for particular Ends; we cannot expect to do, or obtain such things now. Nothing is too big for true Faith to obtain, but that Faith must have a Promise to lean upon, and it must be shewed by <ns0:hi>Prayer,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> adds, that it must be also attended with <ns0:hi>Charity,</ns0:hi> a Chari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />table Heart ready to forgive, and Actually forgiving our Bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren their Trespasses: But it is no more th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>n we met with in <ns0:hi>Matthew, Ch.</ns0:hi> 6. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14, 15. where we opened the Sense of those Words.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>

Luk. 20.1.</ns0:note> And when he was come into the Temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people, came unto him, as he was teaching, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 2.14. Act. 4.7 <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 7.27.</ns0:note> said, By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> hath before this, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 11.18. <ns0:hi>And the Scribes and chief Priests heard it:</ns0:hi> That is, his turning the Buyers and Sellers out, and overturning the Tables of the Money Chan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gers, <ns0:hi>and sought how they might destroy him: For they feared him, because all the People was astonished at his Doctrine.</ns0:hi> Then <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 27. he saith, <ns0:hi>And they came again to Ierusalem, and as he was walking in the Temple, there came to him the Chief Priests, and the Scribes, and the Elders: And say unto him, By what Authority doest thou these things? And who gave thee this Authority to do these things? Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 19.47.48. <ns0:hi>And he taught daily in the Temple, but the Chief Priests, and the Scribes, and the Chief of the People sought to destroy him: And could not find what they might do, for all the People were very <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ttentive to hear him.</ns0:hi> It is plain that our Saviour went <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ver<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Night to <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> and returned to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> every Mor<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>ing, and daily Preached in the Temple. And <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the People were very <ns0:hi>Attentive to hear him.</ns0:hi> In the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> it is, <ns0:hi>

                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                        </ns0:gap>pon him,</ns0:hi> hearing him. They were also much affect<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed with the Miracles, which they had seen him working: So as the <ns0:hi>Scribes,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Elders</ns0:hi> feared him (saith <ns0:hi>Mark.</ns0:hi>) This possibly might be one reason, why they made no opposition to our Saviour, <ns0:hi>driving the Buyers and Sellers out of the Temple.</ns0:hi> viz. For fear of the People; for we must remem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber they were a conquered Tributary People, and under the Jurisdiction of the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> under whom, tho they had a Liberty for the Exercise of their own Religion, yet they had not such a Power as before: <ns0:hi>It was not Lawful for them to put any to Death, Ioh.</ns0:hi> 18.31. And for the preser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving of their own Liberty, they were obliged to take heed, of causing any Tumults for matters concerning their Religi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on. So as what they did of this Nature, they did by <ns0:hi>Craf<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi> rather than plainly, and openly Attempting it. <ns0:hi>Mar</ns0:hi> 14.1. It is likely, they might have some previous, secret Councels, what Method to take, mentioned both by <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi>: The Method it seems which they agreed upon, was first to send to him, to know, <ns0:hi>By what Authority he did th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>se things, and who gave him such Authority?</ns0:hi> This is mentioned both by <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark,</ns0:hi> they sent such a Message to <ns0:hi>Iohn, Ch.</ns0:hi> 1.19, 20, 21. They had often questioned him about his <ns0:hi>Doctrine,</ns0:hi> and had gone by the worst, he justifying his <ns0:hi>Doctrine</ns0:hi> to their Faces. For the Truth of his Miracles, it was so Evident that they could not question that: They therefore now only question his <ns0:hi>Authority</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Preach.</ns0:hi> The Question was Captious enough, for if he had said by a <ns0:hi>Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Authority,</ns0:hi> they would probably have accused him of <ns0:hi>Blasphemy</ns0:hi>: For an <ns0:hi>Humane Authority,</ns0:hi> they knew he had none, according to their Rules for Order, for they came from the <ns0:hi>Court,</ns0:hi> that should have given them such Authority: Our Saviour well enough understanding their Design, gives them, who would not understand his Divine Mission by his miraculous Operations, a wary Answer.</ns0:note>
